"Fixed = H alstead and L uria (two big standard kits); flexible = pick-by-hypothesis." MMSE 24 , MoCA 26 (MoCA is the harder, higher bar, alphabetically and numerically later). 7. Amnesia types & memory disorders Lead fact: the whole topic is anchored to one reference point, the moment of injury. Anterograde = cannot form NEW memories AFTER the event (the clock runs forward, the past is intact). Retrograde = loss of OLD memories from BEFORE the event (the clock runs backward into the past). H.M. is the classic anterograde case (bilateral medial temporal lobe / hippocampus removed for epilepsy). Most real organic amnesias are mixed but anterograde-dominant; pure retrograde amnesia is rare and raises suspicion of a functional (psychogenic) cause. The underlying logic the examiner tests: the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe are needed to consolidate new declarative memories, but once a memory is fully consolidated it is stored in distributed neocortex . So damaging that consolidation machinery wipes out the ability to lay down new traces (anterograde) and the not-yet-consolidated recent past (a graded retrograde loss), while old, well-consolidated memories survive. This single mechanism explains both Ribot's gradient and why H.M. kept his childhood but not his afternoon. Anterograde amnesia Retrograde amnesia What is lost New memories cannot be formed after the event Old memories from before the event are gone Time direction Forward from the injury Backward from the injury Memory type hit New declarative (episodic + semantic); procedural usually spared Mostly episodic/autobiographical; graded by recency Classic case / cause H.M.; Korsakoff's; hippocampal / medial temporal damage Head trauma, ECT; often follows Ribot's gradient Typical exam tag "Can't make new memories" "Forgot the past / who they were" Ribot's Law and the temporal gradient Ribot's Law (Théodule Ribot, 1881): in retrograde amnesia, recent memories are lost first and most severely; older, remote memories are most resistant. This is the temporal (Ribot) gradient , summarised as " last in, first out ." The reason: remote memories have had more time to consolidate into neocortex and no longer depend on the damaged hippocampus. A flat (non-graded) retrograde loss, where even childhood is gone but new learning is fine, points away from organic amnesia and toward a dissociative/functional picture. Korsakoff's syndrome and the Wernicke-Korsakoff complex Cause: chronic thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency , classically from alcoholism (also severe malnutrition, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery). Thiamine is a cofactor for glucose metabolism, so deprived diencephalic neurons die. Lesion sites: the mammillary bodies and the dorsomedial (mediodorsal) nucleus of the thalamus ; this is the prototype diencephalic amnesia . Clinical picture: dense anterograde amnesia (plus a graded retrograde component) with prominent confabulation (fabricated answers filling memory gaps, without intent to lie) and poor insight. Wernicke's encephalopathy is the acute, reversible phase that precedes/accompanies it. Its classic triad : confusion (global encephalopathy) + ophthalmoplegia / nystagmus (eye-movement palsy) + ataxia (gait). Treat emergently with thiamine before glucose (giving glucose first can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's). Untreated Wernicke's can progress to the chronic, largely irreversible Korsakoff psychosis : hence Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome . The other named amnesias Transient Global Amnesia (TGA): sudden, temporary, self-limiting episode of dense anterograde (and some retrograde) amnesia lasting a few hours, with characteristic repetitive questioning ("where am I? what are we doing?"). Personal identity is preserved and there is no focal neurology; it resolves fully within 24 hours and rarely recurs. Dissociative (psychogenic) amnesia: memory loss from psychological trauma, not organic injury ; typically a loss of autobiographical / personal identity information, often selective for the traumatic event, and reversible. A DSM-5 dissociative disorder; dissociative fugue (sudden travel with identity loss) is a specifier. This is the key organic-vs-functional split: functional amnesia spares new learning but loses the personal past, often flat rather than graded. Source amnesia: the information is retained but its source/context is lost (you know the fact but not where or when you learned it). Tied to frontal-lobe function and prominent in ageing and frontal damage; underlies "cryptomnesia" (unintentional plagiarism). Infantile (childhood) amnesia: the normal inability of adults to recall events from roughly the first 3 to 4 years of life , attributed to immature hippocampal/prefrontal consolidation and lack of an autobiographical "self" framework. The landmark cases H.M. (Henry Molaison): underwent bilateral medial temporal lobectomy (hippocampus + nearby structures) by William Scoville for intractable epilepsy. Result: severe anterograde amnesia and graded retrograde loss, but intact procedural learning (improved at the mirror-drawing task across days while denying ever having done it). Studied for decades by Brenda Milner ; the proof that declarative and procedural (non-declarative) memory are separate systems , and that the medial temporal lobe is for declarative memory. Clive Wearing: herpes simplex encephalitis destroyed his hippocampi, leaving perhaps the most extreme combined anterograde + retrograde amnesia (a memory span of seconds, repeated "first awakening"), yet he retained procedural skill, still playing and conducting music. K.C. (Kent Cochrane): motorcycle head injury; a striking dissociation in which episodic memory (personal re-experienced events) was lost but semantic memory (facts, general knowledge) was preserved, key evidence for Tulving's episodic/semantic distinction. Memory systems map (what gets spared vs lost) System Subtype Status in classic amnesia Declarative (explicit) Episodic (events) + Semantic (facts) Impaired (the deficit in H.M., Korsakoff) Non-declarative (implicit) Procedural skills, priming, conditioning Spared (H.M. learned mirror-drawing) Diencephalic vs medial-temporal amnesia Medial-temporal amnesia Diencephalic amnesia Site Hippocampus / medial temporal lobe Mammillary bodies + dorsomedial thalamus Prototype H.M., herpes encephalitis (Clive Wearing) Korsakoff's syndrome Hallmark feature Rapid forgetting, failed encoding/consolidation Confabulation, poor temporal ordering, apathy Cause Surgery, anoxia, HSV encephalitis Thiamine (B1) deficiency, alcohol Worked PYQ-style examples. (1) Stem: "A patient cannot recall events from the years before a road accident but learns new material normally." Answer: retrograde amnesia , and because old memories are preserved better than recent ones, that grading is Ribot's law . (2) Stem: "Chronic alcoholic, confused, abnormal eye movements and unsteady gait." Answer: Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia); if it progresses to amnesia with confabulation it becomes Korsakoff's , due to thiamine (B1) deficiency, lesion in mammillary bodies / dorsomedial thalamus . (3) Stem: "After temporal-lobe surgery a man cannot form new memories yet improves daily on a mirror-drawing task he denies practising." Answer: H.M. , showing anterograde amnesia with spared procedural learning (declarative vs procedural dissociation). Trap: "Can't make NEW memories" = anterograde (H.M., Korsakoff). "Forgot the PAST" = retrograde (Ribot's gradient: recent gone first, remote spared). Korsakoff = thiamine (B1) + alcohol + confabulation , lesion at mammillary bodies + dorsomedial thalamus (diencephalic), NOT hippocampal. Wernicke triad = confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia (give thiamine before glucose). Trap: Dissociative (psychogenic) amnesia is functional (trauma, loss of personal identity/autobiography, new learning intact, often flat not graded), NOT brain damage, that is the organic-vs-functional split. Source amnesia (know the fact, forgot where you learned it) is frontal , do not confuse it with anterograde amnesia (where the fact itself is gone). K.C. = episodic lost, semantic kept ; do not flip them. Hook: " Antero = After, Retro = Rear (the past). " " Ribot: last in, first out. " " Korsakoff: COWs Confabulate , Confusion-Ophthalmoplegia-ataxia (Wernicke) then memory + Confabulation (Korsakoff), all on B 1 ." "H.M. forgot the facts but kept the skill ." 8. Item Response Theory (IRT) / Rasch Lead fact: IRT models the probability of a correct response as a function of the person's latent ability (θ, "theta") and the item's parameters . The number of item parameters names the model: 1PL (Rasch) = difficulty only; 2PL = difficulty + discrimination; 3PL = difficulty + discrimination + guessing; 4PL adds an upper asymptote (carelessness/slip). Ability and item difficulty are placed on the same scale , so a person and an item can be directly compared. The underlying logic: latent trait and the logistic link IRT (also called latent trait theory ) assumes a single unobservable trait θ underlies the responses; θ is conventionally scaled with mean 0 and SD 1, roughly from −3 (very low ability) to +3 (very high ability). The probability of a correct answer rises monotonically with θ following an S-shaped logistic function . For the 2PL model the probability is: P(θ) = c + (1 − c) / (1 + e^(−a(θ − b))) where b = difficulty, a = discrimination, c = guessing (lower asymptote). Set c = 0 and you have the 2PL; further fix a = 1 (constant across items) and you have the 1PL / Rasch model, where the only thing that varies between items is difficulty. Model Parameters estimated Key idea 1PL / Rasch b = difficulty only (a fixed = 1, c = 0) All items assumed equally discriminating; only difficulty varies. The Rasch tradition treats this as a measurement requirement (items must fit the model), not just a convenience. 2PL b = difficulty, a = discrimination Items differ in how sharply they separate high- from low-ability people. The data fit the model (rather than the model being imposed). 3PL b , a , and c = guessing (lower asymptote) Adds a pseudo-chance/guessing parameter, e.g. about 0.20 to 0.25 on a 4 to 5-option MCQ, so even very low-ability examinees have a non-zero chance. 4PL b , a , c , and d = upper asymptote Rarely used; d caps the curve below 1.0 to model "slips"/carelessness so even high-ability people occasionally miss. Reading the Item Characteristic Curve (ICC) The ICC is the S-shaped (logistic) curve plotting P(correct) on the y-axis against ability θ on the x-axis. Each item has its own ICC. Difficulty (b) = horizontal shift. It is the value of θ at which P = 0.5 (for the 2PL; for the 3PL it is the inflection point, where P = (1+c)/2). A harder item shifts the whole curve to the right (you need more θ to reach 50% chance); an easy item sits to the left. Discrimination (a) = slope/steepness of the curve at its inflection point. A steep curve sharply separates people just below vs just above b; a flat curve barely distinguishes ability levels (poor discrimination). Guessing (c) = lower asymptote , the height of the left tail where the curve flattens above zero. It is the floor probability for very low θ. Carelessness (d) = upper asymptote (4PL only), the ceiling below 1.0 on the right tail. Item and Test Information Functions IRT reframes precision through information rather than a single reliability coefficient. The Item Information Function (IIF) shows how much an item reduces measurement error at each level of θ. An item gives maximum information near θ = its own difficulty b , and a higher discrimination (a) yields a taller, narrower information peak . The Test Information Function (TIF) is simply the sum of the item information functions, so a test built from items spread across difficulties measures well over a wide ability range. Information relates inversely to the Standard Error of measurement of θ : SE(θ) = 1 / √(Information(θ)) This is IRT's key advantage: precision is conditional on θ (the test can be precise for mid-range examinees but vague at the extremes), unlike CTT's single SEM applied to every score. Core assumptions Unidimensionality: one dominant latent trait accounts for the responses. Local (conditional) independence: once θ is held constant, responses to different items are statistically independent; an examinee's answer to item 2 is not influenced by item 1 beyond their shared dependence on θ. (Violated by "testlets", e.g. several questions hanging off one reading passage.) Correct model fit / monotonicity: P(correct) rises monotonically with θ, and the chosen model (1PL/2PL/3PL) actually fits the data. IRT vs Classical Test Theory (CTT): invariance is the selling point Feature Classical Test Theory (CTT) Item Response Theory (IRT) Item statistics (difficulty p, discrimination) Sample-dependent : p and item-total correlations change with the sample's ability. Sample-invariant : item parameters are theoretically stable across groups. Person score Raw/true score is test-dependent (depends on which items were used). θ is test-independent : estimated on a common scale regardless of which items the person took. Unit of analysis The whole test (reliability is a single number). The individual item (information is conditional on θ). Precision One SEM for all scores. SE(θ) varies across the ability range. This invariance / sample-independence property (item parameters do not depend on the particular sample, and ability does not depend on the particular items) is the textbook (Anastasi & Urbina; Singh) reason IRT is preferred for building scalable tests, even though it demands much larger samples and stronger assumptions than CTT. Why it matters: CAT and equating Computer-Adaptive Testing (CAT): because items and persons share one θ scale, the computer can pick the next item whose difficulty b matches the examinee's current θ estimate (maximising information), so a precise score is reached with fewer items. Examinees effectively sit different item sets yet receive comparable scores. Test equating / linking: invariant item parameters let different test forms be placed on a common scale (via anchor/common items), so scores from different forms or years are interchangeable. This underpins modern large-scale testing and item banking. Trap: " Rasch = 1-parameter (difficulty only)." Count the parameters: 1PL→b, 2PL→b+a, 3PL→b+a+c (c = guessing), 4PL→ adds d (carelessness). On the ICC, difficulty = horizontal position (θ at P=0.5), discrimination = slope/steepness , guessing = lower asymptote . Do not flip these. Trap (Rasch vs 2PL philosophy): In 2PL the model is chosen to fit the data ; in the Rasch model the data are required to fit the model (items that vary in discrimination are seen as misfitting and may be dropped). That is why some say "Rasch is not just 1PL with extra rules." Trap (information vs reliability): CTT gives one reliability/SEM for the whole test; IRT gives a Test Information Function so precision is conditional on θ . Higher information = lower SE(θ) at that ability level. Hook: " b -difficulty shifts the curve sideways, a -discrimination tilts the slope, c -guessing lifts the floor, d -carelessness drops the ceiling." IRT's one-word edge over CTT = invariance (items don't care about the sample; people don't care about the items). Information peaks where b ≈ θ, which is exactly why CAT serves you items at your own level. 9. Item analysis formulae (difficulty & discrimination) Lead fact: Item difficulty index (p) = proportion who answered the item correctly. Counter-intuitively, a higher p means an EASIER item (more people got it right). The ideal range is roughly p = 0.30 to 0.70 , centred near 0.5 for maximum discrimination. Item discrimination (D) = p upper − p lower using the top vs bottom 27% ; negative D means discard the item. Item difficulty index (p) p = (number who answered correctly) / (total number of examinees) Range 0 to 1. High p = easy item; low p = hard item. The label "difficulty" runs backwards from intuition (it is really an "easiness" index). p near 0.5 maximises differentiation because variance of a proportion, p(1−p), is greatest at 0.5, so the item splits the group most evenly. Acceptable band is about 0.30 to 0.70 ; items with p > 0.90 (almost everyone right, too easy) or p < 0.20 (almost everyone wrong, too hard) carry little discriminating power and are usually dropped. The optimal p shifts upward to allow for guessing : the target is set midway between 1.0 and the chance level. For a 4-option MCQ (chance = 0.25), the ideal p is about (1.00 + 0.25)/2 = 0.625 ; for true/false (chance = 0.50) it is about 0.75 . Average test difficulty is usually aimed near 0.5; a spread of item difficulties is kept so the test discriminates across the whole ability range. Guessing-corrected difficulty (when many examinees guess): p corrected = (R − W/(k − 1)) / N where R = right, W = wrong, k = number of options, N = total. Item discrimination index (D) D = (proportion correct in HIGH group) − (proportion correct in LOW group) = p U − p L Rank everyone by total test score, then compare the upper 27% against the lower 27% (Kelley's rule: 27% best balances having extreme groups against having enough cases). 25% to 33% are also used. Range −1 to +1 . A good item is answered correctly by more high-scorers than low-scorers (positive D). D = +1 means every upper-group examinee passed and every lower-group examinee failed (perfect discrimination). D depends on p: an item with p ≈ 0.5 has the room to reach high D, while very easy (p→1) or very hard (p→0) items are mathematically capped at low D because both groups score alike. This is why mid-difficulty items are favoured. D value Interpretation (Ebel) D ≥ 0.40 Very good / excellent discriminator; retain. 0.30 to 0.39 Good (reasonably discriminating); usually retain. 0.20 to 0.29 Marginal; needs revision/improvement. < 0.20 Poor; revise or discard. Negative D Faulty item : low-scorers outperform high-scorers (usually mis-keyed, ambiguous, or testing a misconception). Always discard and recheck the key. Point-biserial correlation (the other discrimination statistic) The point-biserial (r pb ) correlates a dichotomous item (right = 1, wrong = 0) with the continuous total score . Unlike D (which uses only the extreme 27% groups), r pb uses all examinees, so it is the more statistically stable discrimination index. r pb = ((M 1 − M 0 ) / s t ) × √(p·q) where M 1 = mean total score of those who got the item right, M 0 = mean of those who got it wrong, s t = SD of total scores, p = proportion right, q = 1 − p. A positive r pb (commonly ≥ 0.20 to 0.30 desired) means the item agrees with the test as a whole; a negative r pb flags the same problem as a negative D. Trap (D vs r pb vs biserial): D = upper 27% minus lower 27% (a simple difference). Point-biserial = correlation of a genuinely dichotomous item with total score (uses everyone). Biserial correlation assumes the dichotomy reflects an underlying continuous, normally distributed trait artificially cut in two; biserial is always a bit larger than point-biserial. Distractor / option analysis Examine each wrong option (distractor) by ability group. A functional distractor is chosen by more low-scorers than high-scorers (it plausibly pulls the weak). A distractor chosen by nobody (or almost nobody) is non-functional : not plausible, contributes nothing, and should be revised or replaced. A distractor that attracts more high-scorers than low-scorers signals a flawed item, often a mis-keyed item or a partially-correct distractor; this is exactly the pattern behind a negative D . If too many high-scorers pick a distractor and few pick the keyed answer, suspect the answer key is wrong (miskeyed item). Option pattern (high vs low group) What it means Keyed answer: high > low Good item (positive discrimination). A distractor: low > high Functional, well-working distractor. A distractor: high > low Flawed/ambiguous option or miskey; review. A distractor: chosen by ~0 examinees Non-functional distractor; replace. Keyed answer: low > high Miskeyed item; negative D; discard/rekey. How item analysis feeds reliability and validity Discrimination is the bridge from item analysis to reliability : items that each correlate well with the total score raise inter-item consistency , so retaining high-D / high-r pb items directly increases Cronbach's alpha / KR-20 . Dropping near-zero and negative discriminators lengthens the consistent core of the test and tightens reliability. Selecting items that span the content domain also protects content validity , so item analysis is a quality-control step before a test is finalised. Worked PYQ-style examples Stem: "60 of 200 examinees answered item 7 correctly; the difficulty index is ___ and the item is ___." Answer: p = 60/200 = 0.30 , a relatively hard but acceptable item (at the lower edge of the 0.30 to 0.70 band). Stem: "In the upper group 80% passed an item and in the lower group 90% passed it. The discrimination index is ___." Answer: D = 0.80 − 0.90 = −0.10 (negative) , so the item is faulty and should be discarded / the key checked ; low-scorers outperformed high-scorers. Stem: "A distractor is chosen by more students in the high-scoring group than the low-scoring group. This indicates ___." Answer: a flawed/ambiguous (possibly miskeyed) item , the distractor is functioning against the key. Trap (the most-missed point): a HIGH difficulty index (p) means an EASY item ; the word "difficulty" is backwards from intuition. D ≥ 0.40 = good; negative D = throw it out. Ideal p is near 0.5 but is nudged upward to offset guessing (about 0.625 for 4-option MCQs). Trap (difficulty vs discrimination ceiling): very easy (p→1) and very hard (p→0) items cannot discriminate well, their D is mathematically squeezed toward 0, so p and D are linked, not independent. Hook: " p is popularity (high p = easy); D is the difference (upper minus lower, top/bottom 27% )." "Negative D = nuke the item." "A distractor should fish for the weak : low > high is healthy, high > low is a red flag." 10. Sampling methods (identify from the scenario) Lead fact: the master split is probability sampling (every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection, the selection is random so the sample is unbiased in expectation, generalisation is justified and sampling error can be estimated ) vs non-probability sampling (selection by convenience, judgement or quota, so the probability of selection is unknown, sampling error cannot be estimated , and selection bias is higher). The first decision the stem forces is simply: was the selection random / known chance , or did the researcher choose / take whoever was available ? That settles the half before you name the exact technique. Why it matters: inferential statistics (confidence intervals, p-values, standard errors) all assume the sample was drawn by a random mechanism from a defined sampling frame. With non-probability methods you can still describe the data, but the inference back to the population is informal. Singh (Tests, Measurements & Research Methods) frames probability sampling as the basis for "representativeness by design," whereas non-probability sampling buys feasibility at the cost of unquantifiable bias. Probability (random) methods Method How it works Key feature / when used Scenario cue (the tell) Simple random (SRS) Every unit and every combination of units has an equal chance; lottery method or random-number table/generator Needs a complete sampling frame; gold standard but can be impractical for large, scattered populations "Names drawn from a hat," "random number generator," "lottery method" Systematic List the frame, compute interval k = N / n , pick a random start between 1 and k, then take every k-th unit Quick, spreads the sample evenly across the list; the random start is what keeps it a probability method " Every 10th patient on the register," "every k-th name on the list" Stratified Divide the population into strata (mutually exclusive subgroups) , then draw a random sample within each stratum and combine Used when subgroups differ on the variable of interest; guarantees representation of every stratum, lowers sampling error. Strata should be internally homogeneous , different between "Divided by gender / grade / income, then randomly sampled from each subgroup" – Proportionate Each stratum contributes in proportion to its share of the population Default; preserves population structure "Sampled from each group in proportion to its size" – Disproportionate Small but important strata are over-sampled (then weighted back in analysis) Used to study a rare subgroup adequately "Over-sampled the small minority group so it could be analysed" Cluster Divide into naturally occurring clusters (schools, wards, villages) , randomly select whole clusters , then study everyone in the chosen clusters Used when no list of individuals exists but a list of groups does; cheaper geographically. Each cluster should mini-mirror the whole population (heterogeneous within, similar between) "Selected 5 schools at random and tested all students in them" – Single-stage All units inside the chosen clusters are studied Simplest cluster design "Picked wards, surveyed every household in them" – Two-stage Choose clusters, then randomly sample units within the chosen clusters Cuts cost further; a bridge to multistage "Chose villages, then randomly picked some houses in each" Multistage Sampling in successive nested stages, e.g. state to district to village to household For large national surveys; combines methods at each level "Sampled in several nested stages / levels" PPS (probability proportional to size) Clusters are selected with a probability proportional to their size, so big clusters are more likely chosen, then a fixed number of units is taken from each Equalises each individual's overall selection chance across unequal clusters; used in NFHS-type surveys "Larger areas had a higher chance of being selected" Non-probability methods Method How it works Scenario cue (the tell) Convenience (accidental) Whoever is easiest or closest to hand; no criterion, no randomness "Students in the researcher's own class," "shoppers at the mall," "first 50 who volunteered" Purposive (judgemental) Researcher deliberately picks units that fit a defined criterion or are seen as typical/expert "Selected experts," "chose typical cases on purpose," "hand-picked for their expertise" Quota Set preset quotas per subgroup (e.g. 50 men, 50 women), then fill each quota by convenience/judgement, not randomly "Fill 50 men and 50 women" but units chosen however convenient; the non-probability twin of stratified Snowball (chain-referral) Existing participants refer further participants; the sample grows through social links "One participant referred friends," hidden/hard-to-reach groups (drug users, sex workers, undocumented migrants) Consecutive Take every accessible eligible case as it presents, over a period, until the target is met "Recruited every consenting patient attending the clinic over 3 months" (common in clinical/OPD studies) Sampling error vs sampling bias These are pitted against each other in MCQs. Sampling error is the natural, random discrepancy between a sample statistic and the true population parameter that arises simply because you studied a sample, not the whole population; it is random , shrinks as n grows , and can be quantified (it is the standard error). Sampling bias is a systematic , directional distortion from a faulty selection method (non-random selection, an incomplete frame, non-response); a bigger sample does NOT fix it , and it cannot be estimated from the data alone. Sampling error Sampling bias Nature Random, unsystematic Systematic, directional Effect of larger n Decreases Unchanged (can even mislead more confidently) Can be estimated? Yes (standard error) No Cause Chance of which units fell in the sample Bad selection method / frame / non-response Sample-size logic (the basics tested) Required n rises with greater population variability (larger SD), a narrower confidence interval / smaller margin of error , and a higher confidence level (e.g. 99% needs more than 95%). Precision improves with the square root of n : to halve the standard error you must quadruple the sample ( SE = SD / √n ). Diminishing returns set in quickly. For a proportion, variability is maximal at p = 0.5 , so that value gives the most conservative (largest) sample-size estimate when prevalence is unknown. Cluster designs lose efficiency: the design effect means a cluster sample needs more units than an SRS for the same precision, because units inside a cluster are correlated. Trap pairs: Stratified (probability) vs Quota (non-probability): both build subgroups, but stratified samples randomly within each stratum, quota fills its subgroup targets by convenience/judgement . Random-within = stratified; targets-but-no-randomness = quota. Stratified vs Cluster: stratified samples within every subgroup (you want each subgroup represented; strata are homogeneous within, different between) and takes some from each. Cluster picks whole groups at random and studies all of them (each cluster is a mini-population, heterogeneous within, similar between). Stratified raises precision; cluster lowers cost. Systematic vs SRS: systematic = "every k-th after a random start." Its one danger is the periodicity pitfall : if the list has a hidden cycle whose period matches k (e.g. a ward rota where every 7th bed is a corner bed, or a list ordered male/female so an even k draws only one sex), the sample becomes biased. SRS has no such cyclic risk. Purposive vs Convenience: purposive is a deliberate criterion/expert choice; convenience is whoever is around with no criterion. Snowball = referral chains for hard-to-reach groups. Consecutive = every eligible case in order until quota met (looks rigorous but is still non-probability). Worked stems: (1) "A researcher lists all 2000 employees, randomly selects a starting number, then surveys every 25th name." → Systematic (k = 2000/n, random start, every k-th). Not SRS (SRS has no fixed interval). (2) "From 40 colleges in the city, 6 colleges are chosen at random and every student in those 6 is surveyed." → Cluster (single-stage) . The tell is whole groups chosen and everyone inside studied. If it then said "and 30 students randomly picked per college," it becomes two-stage cluster . (3) "To ensure equal numbers, an interviewer is told to question 25 urban and 25 rural adults, approaching whoever is available." → Quota (subgroup targets, non-random fill), not stratified (no randomness within). (4) "Studying injecting drug users, the team recruits a few users who then introduce their peers." → Snowball . Hook: "Every k-th = systema tic (tic-tic-tic, regular)." "Stra tified = random within strata; Quo ta = quotas but no randomness." "Cluster = grab whole groups and study all." "Snowball rolls referral to referral." "Error is random and shrinks with n; bias is systematic and a big n won't save you." 11. Defense mechanisms: levels & disorder links Lead fact: name the defense from a vignette AND know its maturity level. Highest-frequency single-mark psychoanalytic item across the readable PYQ corpus (projection 22, displacement 15, sublimation 12, rationalization 11). The framework is Anna Freud ( The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence , 1936), built on Sigmund Freud's idea that the ego deploys unconscious operations to keep unacceptable id impulses and the anxiety they generate out of awareness; George Vaillant later rank-ordered them into a maturity hierarchy (psychotic < immature < neurotic < mature) validated longitudinally in the Grant Study. Gabbard's Psychodynamic Psychiatry is the standard clinical source for the disorder links. The mechanism: why the ego defends A defense is an unconscious, automatic ego process that distorts internal or external reality to reduce anxiety arising from a conflict between drive (id), conscience (superego), and reality. Defenses are not pathological in themselves; everyone uses them. What matters clinically is which level a person habitually relies on. Mature defenses optimise both gratification and the demands of reality; psychotic defenses sacrifice reality entirely. Vaillant's key insight is that the same conflict can be handled at any level, and the level used predicts adjustment and diagnosis. Vaillant's maturity hierarchy (every defense in one line) Level Defense One-line definition Psychotic (reality-breaking) Denial (psychotic) Refusing to accept an external reality that is obvious to others. Distortion Grossly reshaping external reality to fit inner need (grandiose / persecutory). Delusional projection Frank delusions about external reality, usually persecutory, projected outward. Immature (adolescent / PD) Projection Attributing one's own unacceptable impulse or feeling to someone else. Splitting Seeing self/others as all-good or all-bad, unable to integrate both. Projective identification Projecting a feeling AND unconsciously pressuring the other to actually feel/enact it. Acting out Discharging an impulse through action to avoid feeling it. Regression Reverting to an earlier developmental stage under stress. Somatisation Converting psychic conflict into bodily symptoms. Passive aggression / idealisation / devaluation Indirect expression of anger (compliance that sabotages); over-/under-valuing. Neurotic (everyday) Repression Unconscious exclusion of a thought/impulse from awareness. Reaction formation Acting and feeling the opposite of one's true impulse. Displacement Redirecting affect from its real target onto a safer substitute. Isolation of affect Keeping the idea but stripping off the linked feeling. Undoing A ritual act that magically cancels/reverses a forbidden thought. Intellectualisation Retreating into abstract thinking to avoid the feeling. Rationalisation Inventing plausible, acceptable reasons for an unacceptable act/feeling. Mature (adaptive) Sublimation Channeling the impulse into a socially valued outlet (aggression → surgery/sport). Suppression Conscious , deliberate postponement of attention to an impulse/conflict. Altruism Vicarious gratification through constructive service to others. Humour Expressing the feeling openly without discomfort to self or others. Anticipation Realistic planning for future inner discomfort. Vignette → name (worked examples) "A man furious at his boss goes home and shouts at his wife." → Displacement (same affect, safer target). "A woman with strong unconscious hostility toward her child becomes smotheringly over-protective." → Reaction formation (opposite of the impulse). "A repressed-anger patient describes a traumatic event in flat, clinical, emotionless detail." → Isolation of affect (idea kept, feeling removed). "A man who is unfaithful becomes convinced his wife is cheating." → Projection (own impulse attributed to other). "A surgeon channels aggressive drives into operating." → Sublimation (mature, socially valued outlet). "After an intrusive blasphemous thought, a patient must tap the table three times to 'cancel' it." → Undoing (magical reversal ritual). "A student who failed says the exam was unfair and the topic useless anyway." → Rationalisation (plausible self-justifying reasons). "A nurse cares for others to meet her own unmet dependency needs in a constructive way." → Altruism (mature). Defense → disorder links (Gabbard) Isolation of affect + undoing + intellectualisation + reaction formation → OCD / obsessional character (the "obsessional" cluster; think rituals and emotional control). Splitting + projective identification + idealisation/devaluation + acting out → borderline PD (Kernberg's borderline organisation). Projection + denial → paranoid PD / paranoid states . Denial (psychotic), distortion, delusional projection → psychotic states (break with reality). Repression + displacement + conversion/somatisation → classical hysteria / conversion (FND) . Regression, somatisation → prominent in somatic-symptom presentations . Trap (the confusable verbs): Displacement = same feeling, new target (angry at boss, yell at wife). Projection = your feeling relabelled as theirs (I hate him → he hates me). Reaction formation = feeling/acting the opposite (hate → over-kindness). Undoing = a ritual that cancels a thought. Sublimation = redirect into a socially valued act (mature). Rationalisation = false but acceptable reasons for what you did. Intellectualisation = retreat into abstract thought to avoid feeling. Isolation of affect = keep the thought, drop the feeling. Sublimation vs displacement: displacement just shifts target and can be maladaptive; sublimation transforms the impulse into something valued. Trap (repression vs suppression): Repression is UNCONSCIOUS and NEUROTIC (you don't know you pushed it away). Suppression is CONSCIOUS and MATURE ("I'll deal with this after the exam"). Examiners love this pair. Also: denial in its psychotic form is reality-breaking, but everyday "denial" of bad news sits at the immature end; context decides the level. Hook: ladder = " P sychotic, I mmature, N eurotic, M ature" → PINM ("pin 'em" from least to most healthy). "Su pp ression is P urposeful and P ositive (conscious, mature); re P ression is P ushed-down (unconscious, neurotic)." OCD quartet = "Isolate, Undo, Intellectualise, React" (I-U-I-R). 12. Emotion theories Lead fact: match the theory to its sequence of arousal, cognition and felt emotion; the order IS the question. The recurring split is whether bodily arousal comes first (James-Lange), arousal and emotion are simultaneous (Cannon-Bard), arousal plus a cognitive label are both needed (Schachter-Singer), or cognitive appraisal comes first (Lazarus), versus Zajonc's claim that affect can precede cognition entirely . Standard sources: Carlson / Pinel for the neuro substrate, any general-psychology text (Atkinson & Hilgard) for the theories. The core debate: which comes first? An emotion has three components: a physiological arousal (heart races, palms sweat), a cognitive element (appraisal or label), and the subjective feeling . The classic theories disagree only about the ORDER and CAUSAL direction of these three. Common-sense says "I see the bear, I feel afraid, so I run/tremble." James and Lange inverted this: the bodily reaction comes first and the feeling is our perception of it. Every later theory is a reaction to that inversion. Theory Author(s) Sequence The tell / one-liner James-Lange William James & Carl Lange Stimulus → bodily arousal → emotion (emotion = perception of the bodily change) "We are afraid because we tremble"; body first . Each emotion has a distinct visceral pattern. Cannon-Bard Walter Cannon & Philip Bard Stimulus → thalamus routes signals so arousal AND emotion occur simultaneously Body and feeling fire at the same time , independently. Thalamic/hypothalamic theory. Schachter-Singer (two-factor / cognitive-arousal) Stanley Schachter & Jerome Singer (1962) Stimulus → undifferentiated arousal + cognitive label from context = specific emotion Arousal is generic; the label you attach (from context) decides WHICH emotion. Lazarus (cognitive-appraisal) Richard Lazarus Stimulus → cognitive appraisal → arousal AND emotion together Appraisal first and it is necessary ; no appraisal, no emotion. "Cognition is necessary and sufficient." Zajonc (affective primacy) Robert Zajonc Stimulus → affect (can occur with NO conscious cognition) "Preferences need no inferences"; affect can precede and be independent of cognition (separate systems). Schachter-Singer: the 1962 adrenaline (epinephrine) study Schachter and Singer injected participants with epinephrine (adrenaline) under the cover story of testing a vitamin ("Suproxin"). Some were correctly informed of the arousal symptoms, some misinformed/uninformed. Each then waited with a confederate who acted either euphoric or angry . Participants who had no explanation for their arousal "caught" the confederate's emotion, reporting euphoria or anger to match the context, whereas those told to expect the symptoms did not. Conclusion: the same physiological arousal is labelled as different emotions depending on the cognitive interpretation of the situation . Hence "two factors": arousal + label. The Lazarus to Zajonc debate (affect vs cognition primacy) This is a favourite pairing. Lazarus argued cognition (appraisal) is a precondition of emotion , even if it is fast or unconscious: you must minimally evaluate the stimulus as relevant before you feel. He distinguished primary appraisal ("is this relevant/threatening to my goals?") from secondary appraisal ("can I cope with it?"). Zajonc countered that affect can arise without prior cognition , citing the mere-exposure effect (we come to prefer stimuli we have merely been exposed to, even subliminally, with no recognition memory) and arguing affect and cognition are separate, partially independent systems . His slogan: " preferences need no inferences ." The exam answer: Lazarus = cognitive/appraisal primacy; Zajonc = affective primacy. Adjacent ideas the examiner pairs in Facial-feedback hypothesis: facial muscle activity itself feeds back to intensify/initiate the matching emotion (Tomkins; tested by the pen-in-teeth "smile" study). A modern descendant of James-Lange's "body first" logic. Plutchik's wheel of emotions: 8 primary emotions in 4 opposing pairs: joy to sadness, trust to disgust, fear to anger, surprise to anticipation . Adjacent primaries combine into dyads (e.g. joy + trust = love); each varies in intensity (a cone). Evolutionary/adaptive framing. Ekman's basic emotions: cross-culturally recognised universal facial expressions; the core six are happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, disgust (contempt later proposed). Evidence from preliterate cultures supports universality. Papez circuit / limbic substrate: James Papez's proposed emotion circuit, hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → anterior thalamus → cingulate → back to hippocampus. The amygdala (fear conditioning, LeDoux's "low road" thalamo-amygdala fast route) and hypothalamus are the key modern emotional structures; the Kluver-Bucy syndrome follows bilateral amygdala/temporal damage. Worked stems (sequence → theory) "A man's heart pounds; he then interprets the pounding as fear" → James-Lange (body first, emotion is the perception of arousal). "On seeing a snake, arousal and the feeling of fear arise at the same instant, routed by the thalamus" → Cannon-Bard . "A person feels generic arousal and, noticing others are angry, concludes she too is angry" → Schachter-Singer (arousal + contextual label). "Whether a forest sound triggers fear depends on first judging it as a threat to one's safety" → Lazarus (appraisal first; primary appraisal of threat). "A person prefers a shape shown subliminally without recognising it" → Zajonc / mere exposure (affect without cognition). "Holding a pen in the teeth makes cartoons seem funnier" → facial-feedback hypothesis . Trap (the four-way sequence): James-Lange = body FIRST (arousal → emotion). Cannon-Bard = SIMULTANEOUS (thalamus sends both at once). Schachter-Singer = needs BOTH arousal AND a cognitive label (the label picks the emotion). Lazarus = APPRAISAL FIRST and appraisal is necessary. Zajonc = AFFECT can come first with NO cognition. Trap (Schachter-Singer vs Lazarus): both involve cognition, so a stem mentioning "interpretation" can fit either. The discriminator: Schachter-Singer requires pre-existing physiological arousal that the cognition then labels (arousal precedes/accompanies the label). Lazarus puts appraisal BEFORE arousal as the cause of it. If the stem says "already aroused, then interpreted" → Schachter-Singer; if "evaluated the situation, which then produced the emotion and arousal" → Lazarus. Trap (Plutchik vs Ekman): Plutchik = 8 primary emotions on a wheel in opposing pairs, with intensities and blends (a structural/evolutionary model). Ekman = basic UNIVERSAL emotions identified from facial expressions across cultures (usually 6). Don't attribute the "wheel" to Ekman or "universal facial expressions" to Plutchik. Hook: order them by how late cognition enters: James-Lange (no cognition, just body) → Cannon-Bard (parallel) → Schachter-Singer (arousal THEN label) → Lazarus (appraisal FIRST). And Zajonc sits outside the line: "preferences need no inferences." Mnemonic for the primacy fight: " LA zarus = LA bel-after-appraisal (cognition first); Z ajonc = Z ero cognition needed." 13. ICD-11 vs ICD-10 / DSM-5: what changed Lead fact: ICD-11 was adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2019 and came into effect on 1 January 2022 (WHO). Its headline changes: several new categories (Gaming Disorder, Complex PTSD, Prolonged Grief Disorder, Body Integrity Dysphoria, Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder), a fully dimensional personality-disorder model (one PD diagnosis rated for severity plus trait domains), and the removal of gender incongruence from the mental-disorders chapter. Two authorities to keep straight: ICD = WHO; DSM = APA (American Psychiatric Association). The logic an examiner tests here is twofold. First, which system a feature belongs to: ICD-11 (the WHO global standard, used for Indian clinical coding) versus DSM-5 / DSM-5-TR (the APA's North-American manual). Second, which edition : ICD-11 versus the older ICD-10. Many "new diagnosis" stems are really asking "is this an ICD-11 addition or a DSM-5 addition?" because the two systems converged on some categories but diverged on others. Read every stem for the body that publishes it and the edition number . ICD-11: the new and relocated categories Category Status in ICD-11 Key point / DSM contrast Gaming Disorder New full diagnosis (in "Disorders due to addictive behaviours," alongside Gambling Disorder) In DSM-5 the parallel "Internet Gaming Disorder" is only a condition for further study (Section III) , NOT an official diagnosis. Complex PTSD (CPTSD) New, separate from PTSD PTSD core (re-experiencing, avoidance, sense of current threat) plus three "disturbances in self-organisation": affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, interpersonal/relationship disturbance. Not a distinct DSM-5 diagnosis. Prolonged Grief Disorder New in ICD-11 Also added to DSM-5-TR (2022) , so both now have it; persistent, intense grief beyond expected social/cultural norm (roughly 6 months+). Body Integrity Dysphoria New in ICD-11 Intense desire to be disabled (e.g. to have a limb amputated), with mismatch between body and identity. No DSM-5 equivalent. Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder New in ICD-11 (classed as an impulse-control disorder , not an addiction) Deliberately NOT called "sex addiction." No DSM-5 category. Bodily Distress Disorder New ICD-11 label Replaces ICD-10's somatoform disorders; defined by distressing bodily symptoms + excessive attention to them. Note the DSM-5 near-equivalent is Somatic Symptom Disorder , and the names are easily swapped (see trap). Gender Incongruence Moved OUT of mental disorders into a new chapter, "Conditions related to sexual health" This is depathologisation. In DSM-5 the parallel term is Gender Dysphoria (still in the manual but renamed from the older "Gender Identity Disorder"). Catatonia Given its own grouping in ICD-11 (not tied to schizophrenia) DSM-5 similarly treats catatonia as a specifier across disorders rather than a schizophrenia subtype. ICD-11 dimensional personality-disorder model (high-yield) This is the single biggest conceptual shift and a favourite stem. ICD-11 abolished the named PD types (paranoid, schizoid, borderline, etc. as separate categories). Instead there is one diagnosis, "Personality Disorder," coded along two axes: Severity first: Mild, Moderate, or Severe (plus a sub-threshold "Personality Difficulty" that is not a disorder). Severity is the primary, most clinically important rating. Five trait domain qualifiers (as many as apply): Negative Affectivity, Detachment, Dissociality, Disinhibition, Anankastia. (Mnemonic order: ND-DDA.) Plus a "Borderline pattern" qualifier retained as an optional specifier (a concession to clinicians and to treatment research built around borderline PD). ICD-11 trait domain Captures (think of the old type it echoes) Negative Affectivity Broad range of negative emotions: anxiety, anger, emotional lability, low self-worth (echoes borderline/avoidant affect). Detachment Social withdrawal, aloofness, restricted emotional expression (echoes schizoid). Dissociality Disregard for others, self-centredness, lack of empathy, manipulation (echoes antisocial/narcissistic). Disinhibition Impulsivity, distractibility, irresponsibility, recklessness (echoes the impulsive pole). Anankastia Rigid perfectionism, control, orderliness (echoes obsessive-compulsive PD). Note this domain is unique to ICD-11 ; the DSM-5 alternative model uses a different fifth domain, Psychoticism. Two related framework facts examiners pair with this: the DSM-5 "Alternative Model for Personality Disorders" (AMPD) sits in DSM-5 Section III (emerging models) and also uses severity + five trait domains, but its domains are Negative Affectivity, Detachment, Antagonism, Disinhibition and Psychoticism (not Anankastia). DSM-5's main text (Section II) still keeps the categorical 10 PDs in 3 clusters. So: ICD-11 main system = dimensional; DSM-5 main system = categorical, with a dimensional model only in Section III. ICD-11 also adds symptom-rating dimensions for schizophrenia and other primary psychotic disorders (positive, negative, depressive, manic, psychomotor, and cognitive symptoms rated for current severity) instead of the old ICD-10 subtypes (paranoid, hebephrenic, catatonic, etc.), which have been dropped . DSM-5 changes (relative to DSM-IV-TR) Dropped the multiaxial system (Axes I to V gone; the GAF score on Axis V was discontinued, with WHODAS suggested instead). Asperger's disorder merged into Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) , a single spectrum with severity levels; the old PDD subtypes were collapsed. Substance "abuse" + "dependence" combined into a single Substance Use Disorder (SUD) rated mild / moderate / severe by number of criteria. The abuse-vs-dependence split is gone. OCD and PTSD moved OUT of the Anxiety Disorders chapter into their own chapters: "Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders" (with hoarding, hair-pulling, excoriation, body dysmorphic disorder) and "Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders." New diagnoses: Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD) (to curb over-diagnosis of paediatric bipolar), Hoarding Disorder (now distinct from OCD), Binge-Eating Disorder, Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder, and Somatic Symptom Disorder (replacing several somatoform categories). Bereavement exclusion removed from major depressive episode (grief no longer automatically rules out MDD). DSM-5-TR (2022) later added Prolonged Grief Disorder and refined wording, but is a text revision, not a new edition. Worked PYQ-style examples Stem: "Gaming Disorder is recognised as a formal diagnosis in which classification?" → ICD-11. (DSM-5 has only "Internet Gaming Disorder" as a condition for further study.) Stem: "In ICD-11, a personality disorder is coded by ___ and ___." → Severity (mild/moderate/severe) and trait domain qualifiers (the five domains + optional borderline pattern), NOT by named type. Stem: "Which trait domain is unique to ICD-11's PD model and absent from the DSM-5 alternative model?" → Anankastia (DSM-5 AMPD uses Psychoticism instead). Stem: "DSM-5 abolished which long-standing feature of DSM-IV?" → the multiaxial (five-axis) system. Stem: "Gender incongruence in ICD-11 is classified under ___." → Conditions related to sexual health (moved out of the mental-disorders chapter). Trap (which body / which edition): ICD = WHO; DSM = APA. Complex PTSD and Gaming Disorder are ICD-11 additions, not DSM-5 diagnoses. Prolonged Grief is in BOTH (ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR). The dimensional PD model is the ICD-11 main system; DSM-5's main system stayed categorical (dimensional only in Section III). Trap (look-alike somatic labels): ICD-11 calls it Bodily Distress Disorder ; DSM-5 calls its near-equivalent Somatic Symptom Disorder . Different manuals, similar idea, do not interchange the names. (Beware also the unrelated old ICD-10 "bodily distress syndrome" usage.) Trap (PD trait domains): ICD-11's fifth domain is Anankastia ; the DSM-5 alternative model's fifth is Psychoticism . The other four overlap conceptually (Negative Affectivity, Detachment, Disinhibition, and Dissociality/Antagonism). Don't put Psychoticism in the ICD-11 list. Trap (DSM-5 substance terms): "Abuse" and "Dependence" are DSM-IV terms; DSM-5 merged them into one Substance Use Disorder with severity. If a stem still splits abuse vs dependence, it is testing the old framework. Hooks: ICD-11 PD domains = "ND-DDA" : N egative affectivity, D etachment, D issociality, D isinhibition, A nankastia (+ borderline pattern). "ICD-11 went live 1-1-22 (1 Jan 2022)." New ICD-11 diagnoses = "Gamers Cry Pretty Bodily Compulsively" : G aming, C omplex PTSD, P rolonged grief, B ody integrity dysphoria, C ompulsive sexual behaviour. DSM-5 = the "de-axed APA" manual (dropped axes; Asperger → ASD; abuse+dependence → SUD; OCD/PTSD got their own rooms). 14. Projective tests: scoring depth (Rorschach & TAT) Lead fact: go past "it's a projective test." Rorschach and TAT recur heavily and the scoring system is the trap . Rorschach = 10 inkblots (5 achromatic, 2 black-red, 3 fully chromatic); Exner's Comprehensive System is the standard quantitative scoring. Standard sources: Anastasi & Urbina, Groth-Marnat ( Handbook of Psychological Assessment ), Singh ( Tests, Measurements & Research Methods ). The projective hypothesis (the underlying logic) The projective hypothesis (Frank, 1939) holds that when a person is given an ambiguous, unstructured stimulus and asked to impose meaning on it, they project their own needs, conflicts, defenses and ways of organising experience onto it, revealing personality structure that they could not or would not report directly. This makes projectives idiographic (rich individual picture, disguised purpose, qualitative) in contrast with objective self-report inventories (MMPI, 16PF, NEO-PI) which are nomothetic (standardised items, transparent purpose, normed scores). The two camps differ on stimulus ambiguity, scoring objectivity, and how easily the testee can fake. Feature Projective techniques Objective inventories Stimulus Ambiguous, unstructured Structured, fixed items Purpose to testee Disguised Usually transparent Approach Idiographic (the whole individual) Nomothetic (compare to norms) Scoring Largely qualitative/interpretive (Exner adds quantification) Objective, mechanical Fakability Harder to fake (purpose hidden) Easier to fake/distort Rorschach: structure and Exner scoring Hermann Rorschach ( Psychodiagnostik , 1921), 10 symmetrical inkblot cards : cards I, IV, V, VI, VII are achromatic (black-grey), cards II and III are black with red , and cards VIII, IX, X are fully chromatic (pastel/colour). Administered in two phases: a free-association/response phase ("what might this be?") then an inquiry phase to clarify where on the blot and what about it determined each response. John Exner's Comprehensive System integrated the earlier rival systems (Beck, Klopfer, Rapaport, Piotrowski) into one normed, reliable scheme. Each response is coded on several axes: Coding axis What it captures Key codes Location Where on the blot the percept is seen W whole, D common detail, Dd unusual detail, S white space Determinants What about the blot shaped the response F form, M human movement, FM animal movement, m inanimate movement, C/CF/FC colour (pure/colour-dominant/form-dominant), Y shading-diffuse, T texture, V vista/depth Form Quality (FQ) How well the percept fits the blot's contours + superior, o ordinary, u unusual, - minus (poor fit, reality testing) Content What the object is H human, A animal, etc. Populars (P) Statistically common responses (conventionality) e.g. the bat/butterfly on Card V Key ratios/indices interpreted from the protocol include the Experience Balance (Erlebnistypus, EB = M : weighted-C) contrasting an inner/ideational (introversive) vs outer/affective (extratensive) style, the F+% / X+% form-quality indices (reality testing), the Affective Ratio , and the Egocentricity Index . The determinant " C " (colour) is classically linked to affectivity/emotional responsiveness ; " M " (human movement) to fantasy/ideation . TAT and the other thematic/expressive tests Test Author / structure Scored on / measures TAT Henry Murray & Christiana Morgan (1935); 31 cards (one blank), about 20 used per testee, selected by age/sex Need-press analysis: the hero 's needs vs environmental press ; apperception = interpreting an ambiguous scene through one's own experience. Reveals motives (n-Ach, n-Power, n-Affiliation). CAT Leopold Bellak ; animal figures (CAT-H is a human version) Children 3 to 10 years ; same apperceptive principle, animals are easier to identify with. SCT Sentence Completion Test (e.g. Rotter ISB) Semi-structured; conflicts/attitudes from completed stems. DAP Karen Machover , Draw-A-Person (Goodenough-Harris for IQ) Body-image / personality from the human figure drawing. HTP John Buck , House-Tree-Person Self, family, body-image themes from the three drawings. Rosenzweig P-F Study Saul Rosenzweig, Picture-Frustration Reaction to frustration; direction (extra-/intro-/impunitive) and type of aggression. Word Association Test Carl Jung (Galton's method) Complexes inferred from reaction time, blocking, unusual associations. Szondi Test Lipot Szondi Choice of liked/disliked portrait faces; largely discredited. Validity / reliability critique Projectives are criticised for low standardisation , examiner-dependent interpretation, weak inter-rater and test-retest reliability for non-Exner systems, and questionable incremental validity over self-report. Exner's system improved Rorschach reliability and norming, but debate over its validity and over-pathologising continues. Examiners may ask which test has the strongest psychometric defence (Exner-scored Rorschach for certain indices, e.g. thought disorder/perceptual accuracy) versus the weakest (figure-drawing "signs"). Worked stems "Ten symmetrical inkblots, two of them black-and-red, scored for Location and Determinants" → Rorschach (Exner) . "The testee tells a story about an ambiguous picture; the examiner analyses the hero's needs and the environmental press" → TAT (apperceptive, thematic). "An animal-figure apperception test for a 5-year-old" → CAT (Bellak) . "Reaction time and blocking to a list of stimulus words reveal unconscious complexes" → Jung's Word Association Test . "A 567-item true/false self-report with validity scales (L, F, K)" → MMPI , an objective inventory, NOT projective. Trap (Rorschach vs TAT): both are projective, but Rorschach is perceptual-structural (HOW you organise ambiguous form, location, colour, movement: a "how do you see?" test) whereas TAT is thematic-narrative (WHAT motives/conflicts your story reveals: a "what story do you tell?" test). Location/Determinant scoring → Rorschach; need-press/hero → TAT. Trap (projective vs objective): Rorschach, TAT, CAT, SCT, DAP, HTP, P-F Study, Word Association are projective (ambiguous, idiographic, disguised). MMPI, 16PF (Cattell), NEO-PI (Costa & McCrae), EPQ are objective self-report (structured, nomothetic, normed). A stem with "validity scales / true-false items / Big Five" is objective, never projective. Trap (author/structure mix-ups): Rorschach = 10 blots (NOT TAT). TAT = Murray & Morgan, 31 cards (NOT Bellak). CAT = Bellak, animals (NOT Murray). DAP = Machover; HTP = Buck; Word Association = Jung. Don't swap Murray and Bellak, or Machover and Buck. Hook: " Rorschach = how you SEE (perception, ink), TAT = the story you TELL (theme, hero)." Card colours: " 5 black, 2 bloody, 3 bright " (5 achromatic, 2 black-red, 3 chromatic). Determinant memory: " F orm, M ovement, C olour, shading ( Y / T / V )." CAT = C hildren + A nimals. 15. Reinforcement schedules (operant) Lead fact: identify the schedule and its response pattern and extinction resistance . Operant content is dense in the corpus. Variable Ratio (VR) gives the highest, steadiest responding and is the MOST resistant to extinction (gambling is the classic VR example). Standard source: any learning text (Domjan, or general-psych chapters on Skinner / operant conditioning). The logic: ratio vs interval, fixed vs variable A schedule of reinforcement specifies WHICH responses get reinforced. Two binary dimensions cross to give the four partial schedules: Ratio vs Interval: ratio schedules reinforce after a number of responses (so working faster earns more reinforcers → high response rates ); interval schedules reinforce the first response after a period of time (working faster does NOT speed the reinforcer → lower, steadier rates ). Fixed vs Variable: fixed schedules have a predictable requirement (so a pause appears right after each reinforcer, the post-reinforcement pause / scallop); variable schedules are unpredictable , so the organism keeps responding steadily and is hard to extinguish. Continuous reinforcement (CRF) reinforces every response: fastest to learn but fastest to extinguish. Partial (intermittent) schedules produce slower learning but far greater persistence , the partial-reinforcement extinction effect (PREE) : behaviour reinforced intermittently resists extinction because the organism cannot quickly tell that reinforcement has stopped. Schedule Rule Cumulative-record shape / response pattern Real-world example Fixed Ratio (FR) Reinforce after a set number of responses High rate with a post-reinforcement pause after each reinforcer (break-and-run) Piece-work pay (paid per N items) Variable Ratio (VR) After an unpredictable (average) number Highest, steadiest rate; no pause; MOST extinction-resistant Gambling / slot machines Fixed Interval (FI) First response after a set time elapses FI scallop : little responding early, accelerating near the interval's end Weekly/monthly paycheck ; studying just before a scheduled exam Variable Interval (VI) First response after an unpredictable time Slow, steady, stable ; extinction-resistant Pop quizzes ; checking for new email/messages Extinction-resistance ranking VR / VI > FR / FI > continuous (CRF) . Variable beats fixed (unpredictability sustains responding); within that, the gambling-type VR is the prototype of dogged, extinction-resistant behaviour. Restated: ratio > interval for response RATE (number-contingent drives speed); variable > fixed for STEADINESS and persistence (unpredictability removes pauses and slows extinction). Adjacent operant concepts the examiner pairs in Shaping: reinforcing successive approximations to a target behaviour (method of successive approximation). Chaining: linking a sequence of behaviours where each response is the cue for the next; built by forward or (often more effective) backward chaining. Premack principle: a high-probability behaviour reinforces a low-probability one ("eat your vegetables, then you may play"); "Grandma's rule." The response-deprivation hypothesis is its refinement. Primary vs secondary (conditioned) reinforcers: primary satisfy biological needs (food, water); secondary acquire value by pairing (money, tokens, praise). A generalized reinforcer (money/tokens) is exchangeable for many primaries. Reinforcement vs punishment (the 2x2): positive reinforcement = add a pleasant stimulus to increase behaviour; negative reinforcement = remove an aversive stimulus to increase behaviour (escape/avoidance) (NOT punishment); positive punishment = add an aversive stimulus to decrease behaviour; negative punishment / omission = remove a pleasant stimulus (time-out, response cost) to decrease behaviour. Token economy: applies secondary/generalized reinforcers (tokens) on a defined schedule, later exchanged for backup reinforcers; used in wards/classrooms. Worked stems "A slot machine pays out after an unpredictable number of pulls; the gambler plays persistently and is very hard to stop" → Variable Ratio (highest rate, most extinction-resistant). "A factory worker is paid for every 20 garments sewn and pauses briefly after each payment" → Fixed Ratio (note the post-reinforcement pause). "Employees work little early in the month and intensify effort just before the monthly salary date" → Fixed Interval (the scallop). "Students study steadily because quizzes can occur on any unannounced day" → Variable Interval . "A child is allowed video games only after finishing homework" → Premack principle . "A rat's lever-pressing is built up by reinforcing closer and closer approximations" → shaping . "Turning off an annoying buzzer by fastening the seatbelt increases seatbelt use" → negative reinforcement (removing an aversive stimulus), NOT punishment. Trap (ratio vs interval): Ratio = based on NUMBER of responses → higher response rates (the organism can speed up the reinforcer). Interval = based on TIME elapsed → lower, steadier rates (speeding up does not help). If "after N responses" → ratio; if "first response after T time" → interval. Trap (fixed vs variable): Fixed = predictable → a post-reinforcement pause (FR) or scallop (FI) appears. Variable = unpredictable → steady responding and greatest extinction resistance . So FI shows the scallop, VR shows no pause; never call the scallop a VR pattern. Trap (negative reinforcement vs punishment): negative reinforcement INCREASES behaviour by removing an aversive stimulus (escape/avoidance). Punishment DECREASES behaviour. "Negative" only means a stimulus is subtracted, not that the effect is bad. Negative punishment (omission/time-out/response cost) removes a pleasant stimulus to decrease behaviour: opposite of negative reinforcement. Hook: " Ratio = Rate (number drives speed); Variable = Vigorous & unstoppable (steady, extinction-proof)." Examples: " gambling = VR, paycheck = FI, pop quiz = VI, piece-work = FR ." Extinction ladder: " Variable beats Fixed; intermittent beats continuous " → VR/VI > FR/FI > CRF. 16. Reliability & validity: every type Lead fact: name the type from its definition. Reliability = consistency/repeatability; validity = measuring what you intend. A test can be reliable but invalid (consistently wrong), but it cannot be valid without being reliable: reliability caps validity (validity ≤ √reliability). Reliability is a necessary but not sufficient condition for validity. Reliability: the logic Classical test theory says an observed score = true score + error . Reliability is the proportion of score variance that is true (systematic) rather than random error . Each reliability method targets a different source of error : time, form, internal heterogeneity, or rater. Conventionally ≥ 0.70 is acceptable for research/group decisions, ≥ 0.80 to 0.90+ for individual high-stakes decisions. Reliability type What it checks Error source / coefficient Key caution Test-retest (stability) Same test given twice to the same people; correlate the two sets of scores. Error over time ; coefficient of stability. Carryover/practice/memory effects if the interval is short; real trait change if too long. Parallel / alternate-forms (equivalence) Two equivalent versions (matched content/difficulty) given to the same people. Error from item sampling (which items); coefficient of equivalence. Hard to build two truly parallel forms. Combine with a delay = stability-and-equivalence (the most rigorous). Split-half Score two halves (usually odd vs even items) of one administration and correlate them. Internal consistency from one sitting (no time/form error). Correlates only half-length tests, so it underestimates reliability; must be corrected by Spearman-Brown . Cronbach's alpha Average of all possible split-halves; inter-item consistency for continuous/polytomous (e.g. Likert) items. Internal consistency / item homogeneity. Rises with test length and with item intercorrelation, so a high alpha can reflect length or redundancy, not a single construct. KR-20 Special case of alpha for dichotomous (right/wrong) items. Internal consistency, varied item difficulty. Use when items differ in difficulty. KR-21 Simplified KR-20 assuming all items have equal difficulty . Internal consistency, quick estimate. Gives a lower-bound estimate; only valid if difficulties are similar. Inter-rater (inter-scorer) Agreement between two or more raters scoring the same responses. Error from the scorer (subjectivity). Use Cohen's kappa for categorical agreement (corrects for chance); ICC or Pearson for continuous ratings. Spearman-Brown and KR formulae Spearman-Brown "prophecy" formula corrects split-half (and predicts reliability after changing test length): r whole = (2 × r half ) / (1 + r half ) (the doubling case) General: r new = (n × r) / (1 + (n − 1)r) , where n = factor by which the test length changes. Kuder-Richardson 20: KR-20 = (k/(k−1)) × (1 − Σp i q i / s²) , where k = number of items, p i q i = variance of each dichotomous item, s² = total score variance. Standard Error of Measurement (SEM) SEM converts reliability into the error band around an individual score : how much an observed score would wobble on repeated testing. SEM = SD × √(1 − r xx ) , where SD = test score SD and r xx = reliability. Higher reliability → smaller SEM (less measurement error). If reliability = 1.0, SEM = 0; if reliability = 0, SEM = the full SD. A 95% confidence interval for the true score is roughly observed score ± 1.96 × SEM (about ±2 SEM). The reliability ↔ validity relationship Random error lowers both reliability and the ceiling on validity, so validity coefficient ≤ √(reliability of test) (more strictly, ≤ √(r test × r criterion ): "attenuation"). Reliable but invalid is possible: a bathroom scale 2 kg out reads consistently (reliable) but never your true weight (invalid). Valid but unreliable is impossible ; if it measures the right thing it must do so consistently. So: reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. Validity: the logic and every type Validity type What it checks How it is established Face Whether the test looks like it measures the trait (to the test-taker/layperson). Subjective judgement; weakest , not real statistical validity. Content Whether items cover the whole domain of the construct (representative sampling of content). Expert review / blueprint; key for achievement & educational tests. Criterion: Concurrent Correlation with a criterion measured at the SAME time . Test and criterion gathered now (e.g. new depression scale vs existing diagnosis today). Criterion: Predictive Correlation with a criterion measured LATER . Test now predicts future outcome (e.g. entrance exam predicting later GPA). Construct: Convergent Correlates with measures of the same/related construct. High correlation with established related tests. Construct: Discriminant (divergent) Does NOT correlate with measures of unrelated constructs. Low correlation with conceptually different tests (Campbell & Fiske multitrait-multimethod matrix). Incremental Whether the test adds predictive power over and above existing measures. Improvement in prediction when the test is added to the battery. Ecological Whether results generalise to real-world everyday functioning. Performance predicts real-life behaviour (key in neuropsychology). Many modern texts treat construct validity as the overarching concept , with content and criterion evidence as contributing sources rather than separate "kinds". Internal vs external validity (of a study/design) Internal validity External validity Question Did the IV truly cause the change in the DV (no confounds)? Do the findings generalise to other people, settings, times? Threatened by History, maturation, testing, instrumentation, statistical regression, selection, mortality/attrition, diffusion. Unrepresentative sample, artificial setting, reactivity (Hawthorne), interaction of treatment with selection/setting. Boosted by Randomisation, control groups, standardisation. Representative sampling, naturalistic/field settings, replication. There is usually a trade-off : tight lab control raises internal validity but can lower external validity. Worked PYQ-style examples Stem: "A new anxiety scale is correlated with clinicians' ratings collected on the same day. This is ___ validity." Answer: concurrent (criterion measured at the same time). Stem: "A scale correlates highly with other anxiety measures but weakly with depression measures." Answer: convergent + discriminant evidence = construct validity. Stem: "Test SD = 10, reliability = 0.84. SEM = ___." Answer: 10 × √(1 − 0.84) = 10 × √0.16 = 10 × 0.4 = 4 . Trap (concurrent vs predictive): Concurrent = criterion measured at the SAME time; predictive = criterion measured LATER. Both are criterion validity; the timing is the discriminator. Trap (convergent vs discriminant): convergent = high correlation with related measures (it converges with what it should); discriminant/divergent = LOW correlation with unrelated measures (it discriminates from what it isn't). Both are needed for construct validity. Trap (alpha vs split-half vs KR-20): Split-half = one specific division corrected by Spearman-Brown; Cronbach's alpha = mean of all possible split-halves (continuous items); KR-20/21 = alpha for dichotomous items (KR-21 assumes equal item difficulty). All four are internal-consistency measures from a single administration. Trap (reliability vs validity direction): reliable but invalid is possible; valid but unreliable is not . Reliability sets the ceiling for validity (validity ≤ √reliability), never the other way round. Trap (internal vs external): internal = causation within the study (confound control); external = generalisability outside it. Don't confuse these with internal consistency reliability, which is a different "internal". Hook: " Re liability = re peatable; validity = veracity." "Con cur rent = cur rent (now); pre dictive = future." " Con vergent con nects; dis criminant dis tances." "A consistent liar is reliable but invalid: reliability is the ceiling, √reliability the cap." Family-systems therapy models (Nagy, Minuchin & the rest) Lead fact: match the model to its signature concept . The shared logic: the family as a system All these models rest on general systems theory : the family is a self-regulating whole that seeks homeostasis , the identified patient's symptom is often the system's way of staying balanced, and change in one part changes all parts ( circular rather than linear causality). Theories of suicide (Durkheim & the psychological rivals) Lead fact: Émile Durkheim (1897, Le Suicide ) explained suicide sociologically , by two social forces: integration (strength of social bonds / belonging) and regulation (degree of social control over needs and norms). Too little or too much of each gives four types: egoistic, altruistic, anomic, fatalistic. His method, treating the suicide rate as a social fact explained by social variables (religion, marriage, war), founded sociological method itself. Durkheim's 2×2 (integration vs regulation) Type Axis & level Meaning Example Egoistic Integration: too LOW Too few social ties; not belonging, excessive individualism. The isolated, unattached, unmarried, irreligious individual; Protestants > Catholics in his data. Altruistic Integration: too HIGH Self dissolved into the group; dies for or with it. Soldier sacrificing self, ritual/honour suicide (e.g. sati), cult deaths. Anomic Regulation: too LOW Sudden collapse of norms/expectations; desires no longer bounded. After economic crash, divorce, sudden ruin, or even sudden wealth ; spikes in boom and bust. Fatalistic Regulation: too HIGH Oppressively over-controlled, blocked futures, no hope of change. Prisoners, slaves (the rarest type; Durkheim mentions it only in a footnote). The psychological theories examiners pair against Durkheim Theorist Core construct The tell Freud Aggression turned inward against an introjected lost object; later the death instinct (Thanatos) . "Self-directed hostility", "murder turned on the self". Karl Menninger Three components: the wish to die , the wish to kill , the wish to be killed . The "three wishes" triad. Edwin Shneidman Psychache : unbearable psychological pain; suicide as escape from it. The 10 commonalities of suicide; founder of suicidology. "Psychache", "common purpose = escape", "common emotion = hopelessness-helplessness". Aaron Beck Hopelessness as the cognitive bridge from depression to suicide (Beck Hopelessness Scale). "Hopelessness predicts suicide better than depression itself". Thomas Joiner Interpersonal-psychological theory : desire = thwarted belongingness + perceived burdensomeness ; lethal act needs acquired capability (habituation to pain/fear of death). Three components; "desire vs capability". Roy Baumeister Escape from self : suicide as flight from painful self-awareness after falling short of standards (cognitive deconstruction). "Escape theory", "escaping aversive self-awareness". Indian epidemiology context India carries a large share of global suicides. Suicide is a leading cause of death in young adults (roughly 15 to 39 years) , with a recognised South-Indian belt of higher rates and prominent methods including hanging, pesticide/poisoning, and self-immolation . Marital and economic stress, and student/agrarian distress, feature heavily. Note Sec 309 IPC (attempt) is effectively decriminalised in practice via the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 , which presumes severe stress in an attempt survivor. These social-structural drivers map neatly onto Durkheim's anomic (economic disruption) and egoistic (isolation) types, which is exactly the link examiners probe. Worked PYQ-style examples "A businessman kills himself days after his firm collapses." → low regulation, norms shattered → anomic . "A soldier throws himself on a grenade to save his unit." → over-integration into the group → altruistic . "A long-term prisoner with no prospect of release." → over-regulation, blocked future → fatalistic . "A socially isolated, unmarried, irreligious man." → under-integration → egoistic . "Suicide arises from unbearable psychological pain." → Shneidman (psychache) , not Durkheim. "Risk = feeling one does not belong AND that others are better off without you." → Joiner's interpersonal theory . Trap (which axis): Egoistic / Altruistic = the INTEGRATION axis (too little / too much belonging). Anomic / Fatalistic = the REGULATION axis (too little / too much control). Cross-pairs are the classic distractor: egoistic is low-integration (not low-regulation), anomic is low-regulation (not low-integration). Trap (egoistic vs anomic): both involve "too little" of a social force, so they get swapped. Egoistic = chronic lack of social TIES / belonging (integration). Anomic = acute breakdown of NORMS / expectations , typically after a sudden change (regulation). Egoistic is about who you are connected to; anomic is about whether your life still has rules. Trap (anomic vs fatalistic): opposite ends of the SAME (regulation) axis. Anomic = norm-LESS-ness, too FEW rules (anarchy of desire). Fatalistic = too MANY rules, crushing over-control (no exit). Anomic is the most-tested type; fatalistic is the rarest. And don't attribute psychache to Durkheim: Shneidman = psychache; Beck = hopelessness; Freud = aggression inward; Menninger = wish to die/kill/be killed; Joiner = belongingness + burdensomeness + capability; Baumeister = escape from self.
