Psychiatric rating scales (CGI, PANSS & the PANSS read) Lead fact: PANSS (Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale; Kay, Fiszbein & Opler, 1987) has 30 items scored 1 to 7 , in three subscales: Positive (7 items), Negative (7 items), General Psychopathology (16 items) ; total range 30 to 210 (each item's minimum is 1, so the floor is 30, not 0). CGI (Clinical Global Impression) is the quick clinician-rated global scale: CGI-S = severity and CGI-I = improvement , each on a 1 to 7 scale. The organising idea: a rating scale is defined by what it measures (which disorder/domain), how many items and on what anchor range , and who rates it (clinician-administered vs patient self-report). Examiners build "which scale?" stems by giving you item counts, score ranges, or the symptom domain, so memorise those three coordinates for each scale. Note that PANSS items start at 1 (1 = absent), which is why every subscale total has a non-zero floor. Clinician CGI-I Global change from baseline Single item, 1 (very much improved) to 7 (very much worse); 4 = no change. The depression pair is the classic: HAM-D / MADRS are clinician-administered , whereas BDI-II and PHQ-9 are patient self-report. Likewise, schizophrenia symptom scales (PANSS, BPRS, SAPS/SANS) are clinician-rated via interview, because patients with active psychosis cannot reliably self-rate. If a stem stresses "patient fills it in himself," it is a self-report instrument (BDI, PHQ-9), not HAM-D or PANSS. Reading a PANSS profile PANSS gives three separate numbers. A profile is "positive-predominant" when the Positive subscale > Negative subscale , and "negative-predominant" the other way. Because PANSS measures only schizophrenia-spectrum symptoms, it carries no mood (depression) and no manic criteria ; you cannot diagnose a mood disorder from PANSS alone. Substance-use screening scales (AUDIT & cousins) Lead fact: AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test; WHO) = 10 items , score 0 to 40 , cut-off ≥8 = hazardous/harmful drinking. It is the WHO's alcohol screener; the very short CAGE (4 questions, cut-off ≥2) is the bedside one. The key conceptual axis the examiner tests: screening (detect a problem) vs diagnostic (severity of a disorder) vs withdrawal-severity (guide detox) tools. These instruments differ along three lines: substance covered (alcohol only, drugs only, or all substances), length / scoring / cut-off , and above all purpose . Screening tools (AUDIT, CAGE, MAST, DAST, ASSIST) ask "is there a problem to investigate?"; a withdrawal-severity tool (CIWA-Ar) does something completely different, it quantifies how severe an already-occurring withdrawal is to titrate treatment. Mixing a screening tool with the withdrawal tool is the single most common trap, so anchor on purpose first. Don't equate "screen positive" with "diagnosed." Hook: "AUD IT has 10 bits, the WHO's audit, cut at 8 ." "CAGE = the 4 -letter cage: C ut- A nnoyed- G uilty- E ye-opener, positive at 2 ." "CIWA = withdrawal , not a welcome screen (it counts the shakes, not the cans)." " ASSIST assists with all substances (WHO)." B5. Verbal learning & memory tests (RAVLT dimensions) Lead fact: the RAVLT (Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test) reads out a 15-word list (List A) over 5 trials , then a 15-word interference list (List B, one trial), then immediate post-interference recall of List A, a ~20 to 30 min delayed recall , and finally recognition . The " dimensions " it yields: immediate memory span, total learning across trials (learning curve), proactive & retroactive interference, delayed recall/retention, and recognition. Full administration sequence Trials 1 to 5 (List A): the same 15-word list is read aloud and free-recalled five times. This builds the learning curve ; normal learners gain words across trials (a typical Trial 1 is about 6 to 8 words rising to about 12 to 14 by Trial 5, age-dependent). List B (interference trial): a new 15-word list is read once and recalled. List B itself serves as a distractor and a fresh "Trial 1" baseline. Trial 6 (immediate recall of List A, post-interference): recall List A again without re-reading it, right after List B. Trial 7 (delayed recall): after a filled delay of about 20 to 30 minutes , free-recall List A again with no re-reading. Recognition: a list (commonly read aloud or as a word sheet) mixes the 15 List A words with distractors (including List B words and semantically/phonemically related foils); the person identifies the original List A words. Yields hits, false positives, and a discrimination/recognition index. Every score / "dimension" and what it means RAVLT score What it captures Trial 1 recall Immediate memory span (attention / auditory working memory; supraspan exposure). Trial 5 recall Best single-trial learning (near asymptote). Sum of Trials 1 to 5 (total learning) Learning rate / acquisition (the overall learning curve and capacity). Trial 5 − Trial 1 Learning slope (how much was gained through repetition). List B (Trial B) vs Trial 1 (List A) Proactive interference : prior learning of List A intrudes on / depresses List B recall. Trial 6 (post-B) vs Trial 5 Retroactive interference : the new List B disrupts already-learned List A (the drop from Trial 5 to Trial 6). Delayed recall (Trial 7, ~20 to 30 min) Retention / consolidation over delay; loss from Trial 6 to Trial 7 = rate of forgetting. Recognition Storage vs retrieval dissociation; also false positives index poor discrimination / response bias. Proactive vs retroactive interference (read it off the trials) Proactive interference (PI): OLD learning hurts NEW. On RAVLT, strong List A learning lowers List B recall (compare Trial B to Trial 1 of List A). Direction: old → new (forwards). Retroactive interference (RI): NEW learning hurts OLD. On RAVLT, hearing List B lowers the immediate recall of List A at Trial 6 (compare Trial 6 to Trial 5). Direction: new → old (backwards). Storage vs retrieval interpretation (the classic item) Recognition intact, free recall poor → retrieval deficit. The information was stored but the person cannot self-cue it; recognition "rescues" it by providing the cue. Typical of subcortical / frontal-executive profiles (e.g. subcortical dementias, Parkinson, depression-related "pseudodementia"). Both recall AND recognition poor → encoding/storage (consolidation) deficit. The trace was never laid down, so even a cue cannot recover it. Typical of medial-temporal / hippocampal amnesia (e.g. Alzheimer-type, Korsakoff). Rapid forgetting (Trial 6 high but Trial 7 collapses) with poor recognition also points to a consolidation/storage problem. Many false positives / intrusions on recognition suggest poor monitoring / source memory (frontal) or confabulation tendencies. Contrast with CVLT and WMS Test List & structure Distinctive read-out RAVLT 15 unrelated words, List A × 5 trials, List B interference, delay, recognition. Learning curve, PI/RI, storage-vs-retrieval. Words are unrelated (little built-in semantic structure). CVLT (California Verbal Learning Test) 16 words drawn from 4 semantic categories (e.g. fruits, tools), List A × 5, interference List B, short & long delay, cued + recognition. Adds a strategy read: semantic clustering (grouping by category) vs serial clustering, learning slope, and use of organisation, plus detailed error/intrusion and recognition (d-prime) analysis. WMS (Wechsler Memory Scale) A broad multi-subtest battery (e.g. Logical Memory stories, Verbal Paired Associates, Visual Reproduction), not a single supraspan list. Index scores (e.g. auditory/visual, immediate/delayed working memory); gives a profile across memory systems, including visual memory, which RAVLT/CVLT do not. Worked PYQ-style examples Stem: "On the RAVLT a patient recalls only 4 words on delayed recall but identifies 14/15 on recognition. This indicates ___." Answer: a retrieval deficit (storage intact, cueing helps), suggesting a subcortical/frontal profile. Stem: "List B recall is markedly lower than Trial 1 of List A. This reflects ___." Answer: proactive interference (prior List A learning intrudes on the new list). Stem: "Which verbal memory test is built from words in semantic categories so it indexes use of clustering strategy?" Answer: the CVLT (16 words, 4 categories), not the RAVLT. Trap (which test): RAVLT is auditory-verbal, 15 unrelated words . The CVLT uses 16 words in semantic categories (so it reads clustering strategy ); the WMS is a broad multi-subtest battery (and the one that covers visual memory), not a single list. Trap (PI vs RI): Pro active = prior learning hurts the new list (Trial B drop); Retro active = the new list reaches back to hurt the old one (Trial 6 drop). Direction of the arrow is the discriminator. Trap (storage vs retrieval): recall down but recognition intact = retrieval problem (cue rescues it); both recall and recognition down = encoding/storage problem (nothing rescues it). This dissociation is the signature RAVLT interpretation question. Hook: "RAVLT = Rey, Auditory, 15 words, 5 trials ; CVLT = 16 words, categories, clustering ." "Recognition saves a retrieval deficit; nothing saves a storage deficit." " Pro = prior hurts new; Retro = recent hurts old." B6. Levodopa & the dopamine story (Parkinson's) Lead fact: Levodopa (L-DOPA) is the immediate metabolic precursor of dopamine and, unlike dopamine itself, it crosses the blood-brain barrier. It is the single most effective drug for Parkinson's disease , in which the nigrostriatal dopamine pathway (substantia nigra pars compacta projecting to the striatum) has degenerated. L-DOPA is always given with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa or benserazide) so that more L-DOPA reaches the brain and peripheral side effects (nausea, hypotension) fall. The synthesis pathway (why L-DOPA, not dopamine) Dopamine is made in two steps from the amino acid tyrosine. The key teaching point is that the final product, dopamine, is too polar to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) , whereas its precursor L-DOPA is carried across by an amino-acid transporter. So you deliver the precursor and let the brain finish the job. Tyrosine → (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate-limiting) → L-DOPA → (DOPA decarboxylase / AADC) → Dopamine Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of the whole catecholamine pathway (dopamine then continues to noradrenaline then adrenaline elsewhere). DOPA decarboxylase (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, AADC) converts L-DOPA to dopamine. It exists both in the brain and in the periphery , which is exactly the problem carbidopa solves. Why add carbidopa / benserazide Given alone, most oral L-DOPA is decarboxylated to dopamine in the periphery before it ever reaches the brain, wasting it and causing nausea, vomiting and hypotension (peripheral dopamine acts on the gut and the area postrema chemoreceptor trigger zone). Carbidopa (and benserazide ) are peripheral DOPA-decarboxylase inhibitors that do not cross the BBB. They block conversion only outside the brain, so more intact L-DOPA crosses, the effective dose drops (by roughly 75%), and peripheral side effects fall, while central conversion to dopamine is untouched. This is the logic behind the combination products Sinemet (levodopa + carbidopa) and Madopar (levodopa + benserazide) . The four dopamine pathways Pathway From → To Role; what its disturbance causes Nigrostriatal Substantia nigra → striatum (basal ganglia) Movement. Degenerates in Parkinson's ; D2 blockade here gives drug-induced parkinsonism / EPS. Mesolimbic VTA → nucleus accumbens / limbic Reward, salience. Overactivity = positive psychotic symptoms ; the target of antipsychotic benefit. Mesocortical VTA → prefrontal cortex Cognition, motivation. Underactivity = negative / cognitive symptoms ; D2 blockade can worsen these. Tuberoinfundibular Hypothalamus → pituitary Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin ; D2 blockade here causes hyperprolactinaemia (galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, gynaecomastia). Antipsychotics: the mirror image of Parkinson's Parkinson's is too little nigrostriatal dopamine, and you treat it by adding dopamine (L-DOPA). Antipsychotics do the opposite: they block D2 receptors. Blocking the nigrostriatal pathway therefore reproduces a Parkinson-like state, drug-induced parkinsonism and other extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) : acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, and (long-term) tardive dyskinesia. Blocking the tuberoinfundibular pathway raises prolactin. This symmetry is the favourite exam pairing: a Parkinson's patient on L-DOPA can develop psychosis (too much dopamine), and a schizophrenia patient on a D2 blocker can develop parkinsonism (too little), and treating one risks the other. Long-term L-DOPA problems Dyskinesias (involuntary choreiform movements at peak dose), as the responsive striatal window narrows over years. Motor fluctuations: "wearing-off" (benefit fades before the next dose) and the abrupt, unpredictable "on-off" phenomenon. Dopaminergic / psychiatric effects: hallucinations and psychosis, impulse-control disorders, plus nausea and orthostatic hypotension. Worked PYQ-style examples. (1) Stem: "Why is levodopa given rather than dopamine in Parkinson's?" Answer: only L-DOPA crosses the blood-brain barrier ; dopamine cannot, so the precursor is given and converted centrally by DOPA decarboxylase. (2) Stem: "Why is carbidopa combined with levodopa?" Answer: carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase (and does not enter the brain), so more L-DOPA reaches the CNS and peripheral nausea/hypotension are reduced. (3) Stem: "Which dopamine pathway degenerates in Parkinson's disease?" Answer: the nigrostriatal pathway (substantia nigra pars compacta to striatum). (4) Stem: "An antipsychotic causes a tremor and rigidity; which pathway is blocked?" Answer: the nigrostriatal pathway (D2 blockade producing EPS / drug-induced parkinsonism). Trap: " Why levodopa not dopamine? " → only L-DOPA crosses the BBB. " Why add carbidopa? " → it blocks peripheral decarboxylase (does not cross the BBB) so more L-DOPA reaches the brain and nausea drops; it does NOT work centrally. The deficient pathway in Parkinson's is the nigrostriatal one, do not answer mesolimbic (that is the psychosis/reward pathway). Trap: match the pathway to the side effect: nigrostriatal block = EPS / parkinsonism ; tuberoinfundibular block = raised prolactin ; mesolimbic = positive symptoms ; mesocortical = negative/cognitive symptoms. Parkinson's = too little dopamine; antipsychotic EPS = too little dopamine by blockade (mirror image), while L-DOPA psychosis = too much dopamine. Hook: " Dopamine can't get in; L-DOPA can. " "Carbi dopa guards the dopa in the periphery so the brain gets it." "Four pathways: Nigro (move), meso-Limbic (psychosis), meso-Cortical (cognition), Tubero (prolactin)." B7. Glasgow Coma Scale Lead fact: the GCS (Teasdale & Jennett, Lancet 1974, University of Glasgow) scores consciousness on three independent responses: Eye opening /4, Verbal /5, Motor /6, summed to a total of 3 (worst) to 15 (best). Severity bands: ≤8 = severe (coma), 9 to 12 = moderate, 13 to 15 = mild. The minimum possible is 3, not 0 (1+1+1), because every component scores at least 1. The point of the scale is a quick, reproducible, communicable number for level of consciousness that any clinician can repeat at the bedside to track deterioration or improvement. Always record the breakdown (for example E3 V4 M5 = 12), not just the sum, because the components carry different prognostic weight, and the motor response is the most powerful single predictor of outcome. Full component breakdown Eye opening (E) /4 Verbal response (V) /5 Motor response (M) /6 4 spontaneous 3 to speech (voice) 2 to pain 1 none 5 oriented 4 confused conversation 3 inappropriate words 2 incomprehensible sounds 1 none 6 obeys commands 5 localises to pain 4 withdraws (normal flexion) 3 abnormal flexion (decorticate) 2 extension (decerebrate) 1 none Severity bands and the airway rule Total GCS Severity Significance 13 to 15 Mild head injury Most concussions; usually observe. 9 to 12 Moderate head injury Needs close monitoring / imaging. 3 to 8 Severe (coma) GCS ≤ 8 = intubation threshold ("GCS 8, intubate"): the airway is at risk, so the patient is usually intubated and ventilated. Coma is conventionally defined as not opening eyes, not obeying commands, not speaking words, GCS ≤ 8. Decorticate vs decerebrate: the motor trap These two abnormal postures are the highest-yield motor distinction and they localise the lesion. Both are responses to a painful stimulus. Decorticate (M3) Decerebrate (M2) Posture Abnormal flexion: arms flexed, drawn in toward the body ("core/cord"), legs extended Extension: arms extended and internally rotated, wrists pronated, legs extended GCS motor score M3 M2 Localises to Lesion above the red nucleus (cerebral hemispheres / internal capsule), i.e. higher Lesion in the brainstem (at/below midbrain, between red and vestibular nuclei), i.e. lower and worse Prognosis Bad Worse (extension scores lower, signals deeper damage) Clinically, a patient who deteriorates from decorticate (flexion) to decerebrate (extension) is "going down the brainstem," a sign of worsening herniation. Limitations and special scoring Intubation: an intubated patient cannot speak, so verbal is scored "T" (V T ) and the total is reported as, e.g., 10T rather than guessed. Periorbital swelling: if the eyes cannot open because of swelling, E is marked "C" (closed) . Confounders such as sedation, paralysis, alcohol/drugs, hypoglycaemia and language barriers all distort the score; record them. The GCS handles young children poorly, hence the modified paediatric GCS . Worked PYQ-style examples. (1) Stem: "What is the lowest possible GCS?" Answer: 3 , not 0 (1 + 1 + 1). (2) Stem: "At what GCS is intubation generally indicated?" Answer: 8 or below ("GCS 8, intubate"). (3) Stem: "Patient extends arms and legs to pain; what is the motor score and what does it indicate?" Answer: M2, decerebrate posturing , a brainstem-level lesion, worse than decorticate. (4) Stem: "Eyes open to voice, confused speech, localises pain, total?" Answer: E3 + V4 + M5 = 12 (moderate). Trap: the lowest score is 3, never 0 . Do not flip the maxima: E4, V5, M6 (motor carries the most points and the most prognostic weight). ≤8 = severe / intubate. Trap: Decorticate = abnormal flexion = M3 (higher, lesion above brainstem); Decerebrate = extension = M2 (lower, brainstem lesion, worse). Lower number = worse. In an intubated patient verbal is T , not 1; with eyes swollen shut E is C . Hook: " 4-5-6 , Eyes-Voice-Motor, top is 15 ; floor is 3 ." " GCS 8, intubate. " "De COR ticate = flexion toward the core (M3); de cere brate = extension, brainstem, worse (M2)." B8. National Mental Health Survey of India (2015–16): the numbers Lead fact: the NMHS 2015–16 was conducted by NIMHANS, Bengaluru (PI Gururaj et al. ) across 12 states . It found a current prevalence of mental morbidity of ~10.6% and a lifetime prevalence of ~13.7% (i.e. nearly 1 in 7 Indians has experienced a mental disorder at some point). The headline policy finding is a very large treatment gap of ~70 to 92% across disorders (around 83% overall). Because it was run by NIMHANS, it is especially likely on a NIMHANS-pattern paper. Methodology (what to recognise in a stem) A nationally representative, multi-site survey covering 12 states chosen to represent the regions of India; a multistage, stratified, random cluster sampling design with probability proportional to size. Adults (18+) interviewed in households; diagnoses based on a structured instrument (the MINI , Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview) mapped to ICD-10 categories. It measured both prevalence and the treatment gap , plus disability, socio-economic impact and health-system/resource data, which is why it functions as a policy document, not just a prevalence count. Indicator NMHS 2015–16 figure Current prevalence (any mental morbidity, excluding tobacco-use alone) ≈ 10.6% Lifetime prevalence (any mental morbidity) ≈ 13.7% Overall treatment gap ≈ 83% (range ~70 to 92% by disorder) Depressive disorders current ≈ 2.7%, lifetime ≈ 5.2% Anxiety / neurotic & stress-related disorders a substantial share of the common-mental-disorder load (in the low single-digit % range) Substance-use disorders (alcohol + other, excl. tobacco) alcohol-use disorders the largest single category among men; a leading contributor overall Severe mental disorders (e.g. schizophrenia & other psychoses, current) ≈ 0.8% High suicidal risk ≈ 0.9% Other findings worth carrying: mental disorders were nearly twice as common in urban metros as in rural areas for several categories; the burden was concentrated in the productive age groups (30 to 49 years) ; and there was a strong association with lower education and lower household income . Resource & spending findings (the "system" half) India's government spend on mental health was found to be a very small fraction of the health budget (well under 1%), with per-capita public mental-health spending in the order of just a few rupees per person per year, a figure the survey used to argue for scaling up. A severe human-resource gap : India has only a small fraction of the psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, psychiatric social workers and psychiatric nurses per 100,000 population recommended by the WHO, which is a key driver of the treatment gap. Trap (the swap): keep current = 10.6% distinct from lifetime = 13.7% ; examiners deliberately swap them. Likewise do not swap severe mental disorders (~0.8%) with high suicidal risk (~0.9%) , and do not confuse the overall ~83% treatment gap with the per-disorder range (~70 to 92%) . Trap (who/what): the NMHS was conducted by NIMHANS (Gururaj et al.) , covered 12 states , and used the MINI / ICD-10 . Do not attribute it to the WHO or confuse it with the older NSMH meta-analyses; and the treatment gap, not the prevalence , is its signature, most-tested finding. Hook: " ~10.6% now, ~13.7% ever, ~83% untreated (round it to 10 now, 14 ever, 80 untreated ); run by NIMHANS across 12 states ." B9. Special hallucination types (functional & friends) Lead fact: a functional hallucination = a real external stimulus in the SAME modality triggers and coexists with the hallucination (hears a voice only while the tap runs , and hears both the tap and the voice). Contrast the reflex hallucination, where a stimulus in one modality triggers a hallucination in a different modality. Standard source: Fish's Clinical Psychopathology (Casey & Kelly); also Sims, Symptoms in the Mind . The core definitions (Fish) A hallucination is a perception without an object , experienced in external/objective space with the full force and clarity of a true perception, and (in the strict sense) not under voluntary control . It is distinguished from an illusion (a misperception of a real external object ), from a pseudohallucination (a vivid image in inner subjective space , lacking the substantiality of true perception, with insight retained), and from ordinary mental imagery (faint, in inner space, voluntary, under one's control). The "special" types below are defined by the relationship to a triggering stimulus or the location/form of the percept; their definitions are precise and heavily tested. Type Definition (the tell) Classic association Functional A real stimulus triggers a hallucination in the SAME modality ; stimulus and hallucination are perceived together (both heard). Stimulus is the trigger, not the percept. Tap running → hears a voice, and still hears the tap. Reflex A stimulus in ONE modality triggers a hallucination in a DIFFERENT modality (cross-modal). Music heard → sees colours / feels a sensation. Extracampine Perceived OUTSIDE the limits of the sensory field (beyond what the sense organ could reach), but NOT a different sense. "Sees" a person standing behind a wall or miles away. Can occur in epilepsy, schizophrenia. Hypnagogic / hypnopompic On falling asleep (hypnagogic) / on waking (hypnopompic). Often normal; classic in narcolepsy . Voice calling one's name as one drifts off. Autoscopic Sees a double of oneself (phantom mirror image), often with recognition it is oneself. "Doppelganger"; parieto-occipital lesions, epilepsy. Gustatory / olfactory Hallucinated taste / smell ; smell is often unpleasant. Temporal-lobe epilepsy aura (uncinate fits); also depression. Lilliputian Sees tiny people/animals/objects (micropsia-like), often with a pleasant/fascinated affect. Delirium, especially delirium tremens ; toxic states. Hygric / kinaesthetic Hygric = hallucination of fluid/wetness ; kinaesthetic = of joint/muscle movement or limb position . Somatic hallucinations; alcohol/drug states. Command Auditory hallucination ordering the patient to act; clinically high-risk. Schizophrenia, severe affective psychosis. Auditory hallucinations: person and form Second-person: the voice talks TO the patient ("you are worthless"). Mood-congruent second-person voices are typical of severe depression . Third-person: voices talk ABOUT the patient in the third person, including a running commentary on his actions or two or more voices arguing/discussing him. These are Schneiderian first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia (also: audible thoughts / thought echo, gedankenlautwerden / echo de la pensee ). Elementary vs complex: elementary = unstructured noises (bangs, whistles, buzzing); complex = structured (words, music, voices, scenes). Hallucination vs pseudohallucination vs illusion vs imagery Feature True hallucination Pseudohallucination Illusion Mental imagery Is there a real object? No No Yes (misperceived) No Space External/objective Inner subjective space External Inner subjective Vividness / substantiality Full, like real perception Vivid but lacks full substantiality As real (it IS real) Faint Insight / under control? No insight; involuntary Insight retained ; not fully voluntary Corrected on attention Voluntary , controllable Illusions are sub-typed as completion, affect (fear-driven), and pareidolia (vivid illusions from random patterns, e.g. faces in clouds, which can be produced and ended at will). Pareidolia is the illusion type most likely to be confused with imagery because of its voluntary quality. Worked stems "Hears abusive voices ONLY while the fan is on, and hears the fan too" → functional (same modality, both perceived together). "Every time the doorbell rings, he sees a flash of light" → reflex (cross-modal trigger). "Insists he can see his brother sitting in another city" → extracampine (outside the sensory field). "Smells burning rubber that no one else notices, just before a seizure" → olfactory hallucination of temporal-lobe epilepsy (aura). "In DTs, sees tiny soldiers marching on the bedsheet" → Lilliputian hallucination. "Two voices discuss the patient between themselves and comment on what he is doing" → third-person / running commentary = Schneiderian first-rank. "Sees a frightening face in the curtain folds at night, corrected when the light is turned on" → illusion (misperception of a real object), not a hallucination. Trap (functional vs reflex): both need a real trigger stimulus . Functional = SAME modality , and the stimulus and the hallucination are heard together (running water → voices, both audible). Reflex = CROSS-modality (a sound triggers a visual or tactile hallucination). The discriminator is purely "same sense or different sense?". Trap (extracampine is NOT cross-modal): extracampine = perceived beyond the reach of the sense organ (behind you, miles away) but still in the same sense; it is about location , not "another sense." Do not confuse it with reflex (which IS another sense). Trap (hallucination vs illusion vs pseudohallucination): Illusion = a REAL object misperceived (curtain looks like a face). Functional hallucination = the real stimulus is perceived CORRECTLY and SEPARATELY, alongside the hallucination (you still hear the tap AND a voice), so it is NOT an illusion. Pseudohallucination = in INNER subjective space with INSIGHT retained (the person knows it is not a real external perception), so it is NOT a true hallucination. One real-object-misperceived → illusion; no object, external, no insight → true hallucination; no object, inner space, insight kept → pseudohallucination. Hook: " Functional = same channel, both at once (tap + voice). Reflex = the trigger reflects into another sense. Extracampine = escapes the field (out of range, same sense)." And: " illusion has an object, hallucination has none, pseudo keeps insight. " Third-person voices arguing/commentary = Schneider first-rank . B10. The Wechsler family & WASI Lead fact: WASI = Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence , a short, quick IQ estimate using 4 subtests (Vocabulary, Similarities, Block Design, Matrix Reasoning) , or a 2-subtest form (Vocabulary + Matrix Reasoning) , yielding Verbal (VCI), Performance (PRI) and Full-Scale IQ. Use it when you need a fast, reliable IQ estimate , not a full diagnostic profile. The Wechsler scales are deviation-IQ tests (mean 100, SD 15) covering the lifespan by age band. The key idea the examiner tests is the purpose split : the full scales (WAIS, WISC, WPPSI) give a complete index profile for diagnosis, while WASI trades that detail for speed (a brief screen/estimate). Modern Wechsler scales moved away from the old single Verbal IQ / Performance IQ split to four index scores , so know the index structure, not just the FSIQ. The family by age and purpose Wechsler test Age range Measures Use WASI / WASI-II 6 to 89 yrs Brief IQ (VCI, PRI, FSIQ) Quick estimate / screen (2 or 4 subtests). WAIS-IV 16 to 90 yrs 11 mo 4 indices: VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI Full adult intelligence diagnosis. WISC-V 6 to 16 yrs 11 mo 5 indices (VCI, VSI, FRI, WMI, PSI) Full child intelligence. WPPSI-IV 2 yrs 6 mo to 7 yrs 7 mo Preschool indices (verbal, visual-spatial, working memory, +) Preschool / early primary. WMS-IV 16 to 90 yrs Memory indices (auditory, visual, working memory, etc.) Wechsler Memory Scale, NOT an IQ test. WAIS-IV index/subtest map Index Core subtests What it taps VCI Verbal Comprehension Similarities, Vocabulary, Information (+ Comprehension supp.) Verbal reasoning, crystallised knowledge PRI Perceptual Reasoning Block Design, Matrix Reasoning, Visual Puzzles (+ Figure Weights, Picture Completion supp.) Non-verbal/fluid reasoning, visuospatial WMI Working Memory Digit Span, Arithmetic (+ Letter-Number Sequencing supp.) Attention, mental manipulation PSI Processing Speed Symbol Search, Coding (+ Cancellation supp.) Speed of simple visual scanning/output The four indices combine into the Full-Scale IQ (FSIQ) ; WAIS-IV also yields a General Ability Index (GAI = VCI + PRI, minus the speed/memory load). WISC-V index/subtest map (note the WAIS-IV PRI splits in two) Index Core subtests VCI Verbal Comprehension Similarities, Vocabulary VSI Visual Spatial Block Design, Visual Puzzles FRI Fluid Reasoning Matrix Reasoning, Figure Weights WMI Working Memory Digit Span, Picture Span PSI Processing Speed Coding, Symbol Search Key change to remember: WISC-V splits the old Perceptual Reasoning index into Visual Spatial (VSI) and Fluid Reasoning (FRI) , giving five primary indices in the child scale versus four in WAIS-IV. WASI vs WAIS, the purpose split WASI WAIS-IV Length Brief (2 to 4 subtests, ~15 to 30 min) Full (10 core subtests, ~60 to 90 min) Output Estimated VCI, PRI, FSIQ VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI + FSIQ + GAI When Screening, re-evaluation, research, time-limited Diagnostic profile, clinical decisions, disability work-up Worked PYQ-style examples Stem: "A researcher needs a fast IQ estimate for 200 participants using Vocabulary and Matrix Reasoning only." → WASI (2-subtest brief form). Stem: "Appropriate Wechsler scale for a 10-year-old." → WISC-V (6 to 16). For a 4-year-old → WPPSI-IV ; for a 30-year-old → WAIS-IV . Stem: "Which Wechsler instrument assesses memory rather than intelligence?" → WMS (Wechsler Memory Scale). Stem: "In WISC-V the old Perceptual Reasoning index was divided into ___ and ___." → Visual Spatial (VSI) and Fluid Reasoning (FRI) . Trap: WASI = Abbreviated (brief screen); WAIS = full Adult scale. One letter apart, opposite purposes. "Quick estimate / 4 subtests / screening" → WASI; "comprehensive adult IQ / four index scores" → WAIS. Trap (age bands): WPPSI 2½ to 7½, WISC 6 to 16, WAIS 16 to 90. Overlap at 6 (WPPSI/WISC) and 16 (WISC/WAIS) is resolved by clinical judgement. WMS is NOT an IQ test , it is the memory scale. Trap (indices): WAIS-IV has 4 indices (VCI, PRI, WMI, PSI); WISC-V has 5 (PRI split into VSI + FRI). Don't list "Verbal IQ / Performance IQ" for current versions, that two-IQ model was dropped after WAIS-III/WISC-III. Trap (Indian child IQ): for Indian children the standardised tests are MISIC (adapted WISC) and Binet-Kamat (adapted Stanford-Binet), not the raw Wechsler, see Part A cluster 1. Hook: " WAS I = A bbreviated and S hort." " WAIS = the full A dult I ntelligence S cale." Indices: WAIS-IV = 4 (V-P-W-P: Verbal, Perceptual, Working-memory, Processing-speed); WISC- V = 5 (the V splits Perceptual into Visual-spatial + Fluid). WMS = Memory, not IQ. B11. Affect attunement & DIR/Floortime Lead fact: Affect attunement = Daniel Stern's term ( The Interpersonal World of the Infant , 1985) for the caregiver's cross-modal matching of the infant's inner emotional state, sharing the feeling , not just imitating the behaviour. Floortime is the intervention arm of the DIR model (Developmental, Individual-differences, Relationship-based; Greenspan & Wieder) , used for autism : the adult gets down on the floor, follows the child's lead , and builds the functional emotional developmental capacities through back-and-forth circles of communication . Stern: the senses of self and how attunement works Stern reframed infancy around a developing sense of self that emerges in layers: the emergent self (0 to 2 months), the core self (2 to 6 months), the subjective self (7 to 9 months, when shared inner states first become possible), and the verbal self (from ~15 months). Affect attunement belongs to the subjective-self period: once the infant can sense that inner states are shareable , the caregiver demonstrates this by matching the vitality of the affect. The matching is amodal / cross-modal : the parent picks out the intensity, timing, and shape of the baby's feeling and re-expresses it in a different modality . The baby gives an excited arm-wave; the mother answers with a rising "yeaaah!" vocal swell that matches the burst's contour but not its form. What is shared is the vitality affect (the dynamic, kinetic quality of feeling: "surging", "fading", "bursting"), not the categorical emotion. This is how the infant learns that inner experience can be communed with another mind. Attunement ≠ imitation: imitation copies the form of the act (baby waves, you wave). Attunement matches the feeling behind it, in another channel, which is why it tells the baby "I share your state" rather than "I can copy you". Selective attunement shapes the child: which affects a parent does (and does not) attune to steers which inner states become part of the shared, knowable self. DIR / Floortime (Greenspan & Wieder) D = Developmental: a ladder of functional emotional developmental capacities (regulation & shared attention → engagement → two-way intentional communication → complex problem-solving → symbolic/emotional ideas → logical/abstract thinking). I = Individual differences: each child's unique sensory processing, regulation, and motor-planning profile (what soothes, what overwhelms). R = Relationship-based: learning is driven through affect within a relationship. Floortime = the technique: get on the floor, follow the child's natural interest and lead , then open and close "circles of communication" (child initiates → adult responds → child responds back = one closed circle), gently expanding affect and complexity to climb the developmental ladder. It is a child-led, relationship-based, developmental intervention for autism . DIR/Floortime vs ABA Feature DIR / Floortime (Greenspan) ABA (applied behaviour analysis) Direction Child-led , follows the child's interest Adult-directed , therapist sets the task Basis Developmental & relationship/affect-based Behavioural (operant conditioning) Format Naturalistic play, circles of communication Discrete-trial training , prompts & reinforcement Goal Emotional/developmental capacities, engagement Specific observable target behaviours / skills Adjacent terms (so you can tell them apart) Term Author Core idea Affect attunement Daniel Stern Cross-modal matching of the vitality of the infant's affect. Mirroring Winnicott The mother's face reflects the baby back to itself ("the mother's face is the first mirror"); Kohut uses "mirroring" for the self-object that affirms the child. Mentalization / reflective function Fonagy (with Target) Capacity to read behaviour in terms of mental states; develops via marked, contingent mirroring . Primary intersubjectivity Trevarthen Innate readiness for face-to-face emotional dialogue with another mind from early infancy. Contingent / serve-and-return (attachment / dev. science) Prompt, matched responses to infant cues; the interactional engine behind secure attachment. Worked PYQ-style examples "Floortime is used as an intervention for…" → autism spectrum disorder (within the DIR model). "A baby bangs a toy in an excited rhythm and the mother makes a matching 'da-da-DA!' sound in the same tempo." → affect attunement (Stern) , cross-modal, not imitation. "Therapy follows the child's lead in play to open and close circles of communication." → DIR / Floortime (Greenspan) . "The therapist runs discrete trials with prompts and reinforcers set by the adult." → ABA , contrast with Floortime. "The mother's face gives the infant back an image of itself." → Winnicott's mirroring , not Stern's attunement. Trap (attunement vs imitation/mirroring): attunement is CROSS-MODAL and about the FEELING (vitality affect) , not copying the act. Plain imitation reproduces the behaviour in the same modality. Winnicott's mirroring reflects the infant back to itself (a self-recognition function); Stern's attunement communicates "I share your inner state". Don't merge the two. Trap (Floortime vs ABA): Floortime = child-led, relationship-based, developmental (DIR, Greenspan & Wieder) ; ABA = adult-directed, behavioural, discrete-trial . Both target autism, so the distinguishing word in the stem is "child-led / follows the child / circles of communication" (Floortime) vs "discrete trials / reinforcement / target behaviour" (ABA). Trap (the attachment-side terms): keep Stern (attunement / vitality affects / senses of self) , Winnicott (mirroring, the face as first mirror) , Fonagy (mentalization / reflective function) , and Trevarthen (intersubjectivity) separate. If the stem says "matching intensity-timing-shape across modalities" it is Stern; "thinking about mental states" is Fonagy; "innate face-to-face dialogue" is Trevarthen. Hook: " Stern attunes to the feeling across senses (vitality affect, not imitation)." " Floortime: get on the floor, follow the child , close the circles (DIR, Greenspan, autism)." " ABA = Adult-directed Boxes And drills ." "Mirror = Winnicott; Mentalize = Fonagy; Intersubjective = Trevarthen." B12. R² in multiple regression (coefficient of determination) Lead fact: R² (the coefficient of determination) = the proportion of variance in the outcome (DV) that is explained by the predictor(s). It ranges 0 to 1 (often read as a %). In multiple regression, R² = the square of the multiple correlation R . R² = 0.36 means the model explains 36% of the variance in the DV; the remaining 64% is unexplained (error/other causes). What R² is, mechanically Regression splits the total variability in the outcome into a part the model accounts for and a part it does not: Total SS = Regression (explained) SS + Residual (error) SS . R² is simply the explained share of that total: R² = SS explained / SS total = 1 − (SS residual / SS total ) . So R² = 0 means the predictors explain nothing (the best guess is just the mean of Y), and R² = 1 means the predictors perfectly reproduce Y. R , the multiple correlation, is the correlation between the observed Y values and the predicted Y values from the whole set of predictors; squaring it gives R². R² vs r r (correlation) R² (coefficient of determination) What it is Strength + direction of a relationship Proportion of variance explained Range −1 to +1 0 to 1 (no sign) Reading "how tightly they co-vary" "what % of DV variability the model accounts for" Link r is the bivariate correlation; R is its multivariate cousin R² = r² in the one-predictor case; = R² (square of multiple R) with several predictors Because R² is a square, it is always positive and is always smaller than |r| for r values between 0 and 1 (e.g. r = .50 → R² = .25 = 25%). A correlation that "sounds" moderate often explains a modest slice of variance. Adjusted R² and why it can drop Plain R² has a flaw: it never decreases when you add a predictor, even a useless one, because any predictor can soak up a sliver of variance by chance. So R² over-rewards big models and overstates fit. Adjusted R² penalises the model for the number of predictors relative to sample size ; it goes up only if a new predictor improves the model more than chance would predict, and it can fall (or even go slightly negative) when a predictor adds nothing useful. Adjusted R² is therefore the honest figure to report and compare when models have different numbers of predictors, and it is always ≤ R². Standardized (beta) vs unstandardized (b) coefficients Unstandardized b Standardized β (beta) Units Raw units of the predictor and outcome Standard-deviation units (z-scores), unit-free Reads as "DV changes by b units per 1-unit rise in X" "DV changes by β SDs per 1 SD rise in X" Used for Building the prediction equation; real-world interpretation Comparing the relative importance of predictors on a common scale Intercept Has a meaningful constant (value of Y when all X = 0) Zero by construction (no intercept) Neither b nor β is the same thing as R². The coefficients describe each predictor's individual contribution (slope); R² describes the whole model's overall explanatory power . In a simple (one-predictor) regression, the standardized β equals the Pearson r between X and Y, and its square equals R². What R² does NOT tell you Not causation: explained variance is still just association; a high R² does not prove X causes Y. Not validity of the model: a high R² is meaningless if regression assumptions are violated (non-linearity, non-normal or heteroscedastic residuals, influential outliers, multicollinearity). Always check the residuals, not just R². Not the slope or the size of effect per unit: that is b. R² is a proportion, not a rate of change. Not which predictor matters: that needs the individual coefficients and their significance tests, plus semipartial correlations. Not out-of-sample accuracy: R² describes fit to this sample and tends to shrink on new data (which is part of why adjusted R² and cross-validation exist). Worked reading of the stems "A model has R² = 0.36 ." → the predictors explain 36% of the variance in the outcome; 64% is unexplained. "Multiple R = 0.60 ; what proportion of variance is explained?" → R² = 0.60² = 0.36 = 36% . "Adding a 4th predictor, R² rose from .40 to .41 but adjusted R² fell ." → the new predictor adds essentially nothing; drop it. "Which phrase = R²?" → " percentage / proportion of variance accounted for / explained " = R² (not the correlation, not the slope). "Want to compare which predictor is strongest." → use the standardized β weights, not R². Trap: R² = variance EXPLAINED , expressed as a proportion/%, not the correlation itself (r/R) and not the regression coefficient (slope b or β). "Percentage of variance accounted for" = R²; "change in Y per unit X" = b; "relationship strength" = r/R. Trap: Adjusted R² being lower than R² is normal and expected , not an error; it corrects for the number of predictors. If adjusted R² is much lower than R², you likely have too many weak predictors for your sample size. Trap: a high R² does not mean a good or valid model, and never implies causation. Check assumptions/residuals first; explained variance ≠ cause. Trap: b vs β. Unstandardized b is in raw units (use it to predict actual values); standardized β is in SD units (use it to compare predictors' relative importance). Don't compare raw b's across predictors measured on different scales. Hook: " R² = variance explained. Square the (multiple) correlation, read it as a percent. Adjusted R² is the honest one (can drop); b/β are the slopes, not the variance." B13. Tests notified in the Gazette of India Lead fact: for certification of disability (under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016 , via Gazette of India notifications), India specifies which standardised tests are acceptable to assess intellectual disability (ID) and specific learning disability (SLD) . The classic Gazette-notified intelligence/IQ tests for ID are the Indian-standardised batteries: Binet-Kamat, MISIC, Bhatia's Battery, Seguin Form Board, Gesell Developmental Schedule, DST (Bharat Raj) , paired with VSMS for adaptive behaviour. The logic the examiner wants is the certification framework , not just a list of test names. Under the RPwD Act 2016, disability is certified by a medical board ; the percentage of disability is fixed by Gazette "Guidelines for assessment". For intellectual disability the law follows the standard diagnostic logic of ID : you must demonstrate both (a) significantly sub-average intelligence (IQ) and (b) a deficit in adaptive behaviour , with onset during the developmental period (before age 18) . One alone is insufficient: a low IQ without adaptive deficit, or an adaptive deficit without low IQ, does not certify ID. That is why the notified kit always pairs an IQ test with an adaptive measure (VSMS) . The notified instruments by purpose Purpose Notified instruments What it establishes Intelligence / IQ (for ID) Binet-Kamat, MISIC, Bhatia's Battery, Seguin Form Board, Gesell, DST (Bharat Raj) Sub-average intellectual functioning (IQ / DQ for the very young) Adaptive behaviour (for ID) VSMS (Vineland Social Maturity Scale) Adaptive-behaviour deficit (Social Quotient) Specific Learning Disability (SLD) NIMHANS SLD Index / NIMHANS Index for SLD , curriculum-based tests, + an IQ test to rule out ID Dyslexia/dysgraphia/dyscalculia profile with average/above IQ Why each test is in the kit Binet-Kamat / MISIC , the two main Indian-standardised verbal-capable IQ tests (adapted Stanford-Binet and WISC respectively) for children who can be tested verbally. Bhatia's Battery / Seguin Form Board , performance / non-verbal options for illiterate, hearing-impaired or language-barrier cases. Gesell / DST (Bharat Raj) , developmental tools (yield DQ) for infants and the severely disabled who cannot do a standard IQ test. VSMS , the adaptive-behaviour half; without it you cannot certify ID no matter how low the IQ. NIMHANS Index , the SLD tool, used after an IQ test has shown ID is absent (SLD requires roughly average or better IQ). The 40% benchmark The RPwD Act introduces the concept of " benchmark disability ", defined as not less than 40% of a specified disability as certified by a competent authority. The 40% threshold is what unlocks reservations and statutory benefits (education, employment quotas). For intellectual disability this maps onto the severity bands (the lower the IQ and the greater the adaptive deficit, the higher the certified percentage). Worked PYQ-style examples Stem: "A child has IQ 62 on Binet-Kamat but age-appropriate self-care and social skills. Can ID be certified?" → No , ID needs both low IQ and an adaptive-behaviour deficit. Without a VSMS deficit it is not ID. Stem: "Which adaptive-behaviour scale is paired with the IQ test for ID certification in India?" → VSMS. Stem: "Minimum percentage of disability to qualify as 'benchmark disability' under RPwD?" → 40%. Stem: "Notified test for certifying a specific learning disability?" → NIMHANS SLD Index (plus an IQ test to exclude ID). Trap: the Gazette-notified ID battery is the Indian-standardised set (Binet-Kamat, MISIC, Bhatia, Seguin, Gesell, DST + VSMS), not Western tests like WAIS / Stanford-Binet on their own. Pair an IQ test with an adaptive-behaviour measure (VSMS), ID requires deficits in both with onset in the developmental period. Trap (ID vs SLD): ID = low IQ + adaptive deficit (uses the IQ battery + VSMS). SLD = average or better IQ with a specific academic deficit (uses the NIMHANS SLD Index ). The IQ test in an SLD work-up is there to rule ID out , not to diagnose ID. Trap (numbers): 40% = benchmark disability threshold under RPwD 2016. Don't confuse this with the IQ severity cut-offs of ID (e.g. mild ~50 to 69), those are diagnostic bands, 40% is the certification/benefits threshold. Hook: "Gazette ID kit = the Indian-made ones (Bhatia, MISIC, Binet-Kamat, Seguin, Gesell, DST) + VSMS for adaptive." "ID needs BOTH brains (IQ) and behaviour (adaptive)." " 40 is the magic % for benchmark disability." SLD = NIMHANS index. B14. Levels of prevention (primary / secondary / tertiary) Lead fact: the classic Leavell & Clark framework (echoed by Caplan's community psychiatry) splits prevention by timing relative to disease onset . Primary = before the disorder starts (reduce incidence : health promotion + specific protection). Secondary = early detection & prompt treatment of disease that exists but is early/asymptomatic (reduce prevalence & duration : screening, early intervention). Tertiary = limit disability, complications & relapse in established disease (rehabilitation). A fourth idea, quaternary prevention , protects patients from unnecessary medicalisation / over-treatment . The logic runs along the natural history of disease . Leavell & Clark map prevention onto the prepathogenesis and pathogenesis phases: before the agent-host-environment interaction produces disease you act on susceptibility (primary); once early pathological change has begun but is sub-clinical you act at early pathogenesis (secondary); once disease is advanced you act on residual disability (tertiary). Caplan (1964) imported the same three-level scheme into community mental health, defining primary prevention as lowering the rate of new cases of mental disorder in a population, secondary as reducing the duration of cases through early treatment, and tertiary as reducing the impairment that results from disorder. Park's PSM is the standard Indian source and keeps the Leavell & Clark labels. Level When (natural history) Goal / epidemiologic effect Sub-components Examples (mental health) Primary Before onset (prepathogenesis) Reduce incidence (new cases) Health promotion + specific protection Mental-health promotion, life-skills & stress-coping education, parenting programmes, school anti-bullying work, suicide means-restriction, reducing alcohol availability, perinatal mental-health support. Secondary Early disease (early pathogenesis, sub-clinical) Reduce prevalence & duration Early diagnosis + prompt treatment Screening (PHQ-9, GHQ), early case-finding, treating a first episode of depression/psychosis promptly, early intervention in psychosis services. Tertiary Established / advanced disease Reduce disability & relapse ; limit complications Disability limitation + rehabilitation Psychosocial rehabilitation , relapse-prevention programmes, social-skills training, supported/sheltered employment, family psychoeducation in chronic schizophrenia. (Quaternary) Any stage, vs the health system Avoid over-medicalisation / iatrogenic harm Protect from unnecessary intervention Avoiding needless labels/medication, deprescribing, guarding against pathologising normal grief. Gordon / IOM subdivision of primary prevention Gordon (1983) and the US Institute of Medicine (IOM, 1994) report subdivide primary prevention by who is targeted , not by timing. This is the scheme now used in modern mental-health prevention and is a favourite distractor against the Leavell & Clark levels. Type Target group Mental-health example Universal The whole population , regardless of risk School-wide social-emotional learning; public anti-stigma campaigns. Selective Subgroups at elevated risk (but not yet symptomatic) Support groups for children of parents with mental illness; programmes for the recently bereaved or disaster-exposed. Indicated Individuals with minimal/sub-threshold signs but no full disorder yet Intervention for adolescents with sub-clinical depressive symptoms or attenuated psychotic symptoms. Trap (the classic miss): SCREENING = SECONDARY , not primary. Screening looks for disease that is already present but early, so it is detection, not prevention of onset. Primary = stop it happening at all ; tertiary = limit the damage once it is chronic . Trap (two different "primary" splits): Leavell & Clark split primary into health promotion vs specific protection (non-specific wellbeing vs a targeted protective act like immunisation). Gordon/IOM split primary into universal / selective / indicated (by population risk). Do not mix the two axes. And note indicated prevention (sub-threshold symptoms, still primary) vs secondary prevention (early but actual disease) is a thin line the examiner loves: indicated = risk indicators / minimal signs but no disorder; secondary = a diagnosable case caught early. Trap (authorship): the three levels are Leavell & Clark (with Caplan applying them to community mental health); the universal/selective/indicated subtypes are Gordon / IOM . Mixing the names is a common MCQ snare. Hook: " Primary prevents, Secondary screens, Tertiary treats the aftermath ; Quaternary protects from over-treatment." For Gordon: " U-S-I = everyone, at-risk, early-signs. " B15. Cortical gyri & the auditory trap (Heschl's gyrus) Lead fact: the primary auditory cortex is Heschl's gyrus (the transverse temporal gyrus), Brodmann areas 41 & 42 , sitting on the upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus . It is the first cortical relay for sound. In a typical option list (Q29) it is the only auditory area and the only primary sensory area ; the other gyri offered are association cortex or belong to a different modality, so they are distractors. Why this matters: examiners build the trap by mixing a primary sensory area with nearby association gyri that handle language or reading, plus a visual gyrus, then asking "which is the primary auditory cortex?" If you know that "primary auditory = Heschl = BA 41/42 on the superior temporal gyrus," and that everything else listed is association or visual, the answer is forced. Tonotopic organisation Heschl's gyrus is tonotopically organised: it carries a spatial map of frequency, the cochlea's place code preserved all the way to cortex. Conventionally high frequencies map medially/posteromedially and low frequencies laterally/anterolaterally . This frequency map is the auditory analogue of retinotopy in V1 and somatotopy (the homunculus) in S1. The primary sensory/motor map (memorise as a set) Primary area Gyrus / location Brodmann area(s) Primary auditory Heschl's / transverse temporal gyrus (on superior temporal gyrus) BA 41 & 42 Primary visual Calcarine sulcus / striate cortex, occipital lobe BA 17 Primary somatosensory Postcentral gyrus, parietal lobe BA 3, 1, 2 Primary motor Precentral gyrus, frontal lobe BA 4 The association-area distractors Gyrus Lobe / BA Function (why it is NOT the answer) Heschl's gyrus ✓ Temporal (superior), BA 41/42 Primary auditory cortex , the correct answer. Supramarginal gyrus Parietal, BA 40 Phonological processing and articulation; part of Wernicke's wider territory and the inferior parietal lobule. Association, not primary, not auditory cortex proper. Angular gyrus Parietal, BA 39 Reading, written-word comprehension, number and semantic integration. Lesion gives Gerstmann syndrome. Association, not auditory. Fusiform gyrus Temporo-occipital (ventral) Visual: the fusiform face area (faces) and the visual word-form area. Wrong modality entirely. Wernicke vs Broca vs primary auditory Do not confuse the primary auditory cortex with the language areas that surround it: Area Location / BA Role; lesion effect Primary auditory Heschl's gyrus, BA 41/42 Basic hearing (detects sound). Bilateral loss = cortical deafness. Wernicke's area Posterior superior temporal gyrus, BA 22 Language comprehension . Lesion = receptive (fluent) aphasia: fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension. Broca's area Inferior frontal gyrus, BA 44/45 Speech production . Lesion = expressive (non-fluent) aphasia: effortful, telegraphic speech, comprehension relatively spared. Note the nesting: sound first reaches Heschl (BA 41/42) for raw hearing, then nearby Wernicke (BA 22) on the same superior temporal gyrus extracts meaning, then via the arcuate fasciculus to Broca (BA 44/45) for production. So "posterior superior temporal gyrus" is Wernicke, but the "primary auditory cortex" is specifically the transverse temporal gyrus of Heschl. Worked PYQ-style examples. (1) Stem: "The primary auditory cortex is located in the ___." Answer: Heschl's (transverse temporal) gyrus, BA 41/42 , on the superior temporal gyrus. (2) Stem: "Which Brodmann area corresponds to the primary visual cortex?" Answer: BA 17 (calcarine/striate), the visual distractor against auditory BA 41/42. (3) Stem: "A lesion of the fusiform gyrus most likely impairs ___." Answer: face recognition (prosopagnosia) / visual word forms, a visual function, confirming it is not the auditory choice. (4) Stem: "Posterior superior temporal gyrus, BA 22, comprehension deficit." Answer: Wernicke's area , not primary auditory cortex. Trap: all four offered gyri are real, but only Heschl's = primary + auditory . Supramarginal (BA 40) and angular (BA 39) are parietal association (phonology, reading); fusiform is visual (faces / word-form). Keep the primary companions straight: primary visual = calcarine BA 17; primary auditory = Heschl BA 41/42; primary somatosensory = postcentral BA 3,1,2; primary motor = precentral BA 4. Trap: do not pick Wernicke (BA 22) when asked for the primary auditory cortex : both lie on the superior temporal gyrus, but Heschl (BA 41/42) is primary hearing while Wernicke (BA 22, posterior) is comprehension. And do not confuse Wernicke (temporal, comprehension) with Broca (frontal BA 44/45, production). Hook: " He schl He ars (auditory, BA 41/42)." "Fusiform = F aces (visual). Angular = reading. Supramarginal = sounds-of-words (phonology), not sound itself." "Primary sensory ladder: 17 see, 41/42 hear, 3,1,2 feel, 4 move." B16. Cluster A personality disorders (schizoid vs schizotypal vs paranoid) Lead fact: Cluster A (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal) is the " odd / eccentric " group. The split your Q31 hangs on: schizoid = the content loner who genuinely doesn't want relationships and has flat, restricted emotion, but NO odd beliefs. Schizotypal = the eccentric loner with social anxiety PLUS cognitive-perceptual oddities (magical thinking, ideas of reference, odd speech and perception), i.e. attenuated schizophrenia-spectrum traits. Paranoid = pervasive distrust and suspiciousness. Only schizotypal sits on the schizophrenia spectrum. The discriminator the examiner is really testing is the presence or absence of "odd" cognition/perception and whether the person wants relationships at all . All three Cluster A disorders share social isolation, so isolation alone tells you nothing. What separates them is the reason for the isolation and the content of the inner life : Schizoid isolates because they are genuinely indifferent to people; the inner life is emotionally flat, not bizarre. Schizotypal isolates because they are anxious and eccentric ; the inner life is full of odd, magical, quasi-psychotic content (but not frank, sustained delusions/hallucinations). Paranoid isolates (or keeps people at arm's length) because they distrust others' motives. Criteria-level contrast Schizoid PD Schizotypal PD Paranoid PD Core feature Detachment + restricted affect Detachment + cognitive/perceptual distortions + eccentric behaviour Pervasive distrust / suspiciousness Wants relationships? No : prefers solitude, genuinely indifferent, a "loner by choice" No close friends, but stays apart from social anxiety + oddness (not pure indifference) Wary and guarded; reads threat into benign acts Odd beliefs / perception? None Yes : magical thinking, ideas of reference, bodily illusions, suspiciousness, odd speech No magical thinking, but bears grudges and suspects exploitation/deception Affect Flat, cold, detached, little pleasure (anhedonic) Constricted or inappropriate/odd affect Often hostile, tense, "humourless"; quick to counterattack Speech / behaviour Normal speech, simply unengaged Odd speech (vague, metaphorical, over-elaborate), eccentric appearance Argumentative, litigious, hypervigilant Schizophrenia spectrum? No Yes (attenuated; shares genetic loading with schizophrenia) No Characteristic distortion (none) Ideas of reference (NOT delusions of reference) Suspicion of loyalty; jealousy of partner The discriminations examiners pair this with Confusable pair How to split them Schizoid PD vs schizophrenia's negative symptoms Schizoid is a stable, lifelong personality pattern with no history of a psychotic episode; schizophrenia's negative symptoms (avolition, blunted affect, asociality) occur in the course of a psychotic illness . The phenomenology of "withdrawn + flat" can look identical, but only one has (had) frank psychosis. Schizotypal PD vs schizophrenia Schizotypal has attenuated, intermittent cognitive-perceptual oddities (ideas of reference, magical thinking, transient quasi-psychotic experiences) but no sustained, frank psychosis (no enduring delusions or hallucinations meeting schizophrenia criteria). It is a personality-level, spectrum condition. Schizoid vs schizotypal Odd beliefs / perceptual distortions: absent in schizoid, present in schizotypal. Schizoid is "cold and uninterested"; schizotypal is "weird and anxious." Schizoid vs Avoidant PD (Cluster C) Desire for closeness. Schizoid does not want relationships (indifferent). Avoidant wants closeness but avoids it from fear of rejection / criticism (hypersensitivity). Same surface isolation, opposite motivation. Paranoid PD vs Delusional Disorder (persecutory) Paranoid PD = pervasive trait suspiciousness without a fixed false belief; delusional disorder = a discrete, fixed, encapsulated delusion. Trait vs delusion. ICD vs DSM placement of schizotypal (high-yield) This is a classic trap. In DSM-5 , Schizotypal Personality Disorder is listed in Cluster A of the personality disorders and is also cross-listed within the schizophrenia spectrum chapter ("Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders"), reflecting its genetic link to schizophrenia. In ICD-10/ICD-11 , it is not classed as a personality disorder at all : it appears as "Schizotypal Disorder" within the schizophrenia / psychotic-spectrum grouping (ICD-10 code F21), explicitly alongside schizophrenia rather than with the personality disorders. So "schizotypal" is a personality disorder in DSM but a schizophrenia-spectrum disorder in ICD. Worked PYQ-style examples Stem: "A man lives alone, has no desire for friends or sex, shows flat affect, but reports no unusual beliefs or perceptions." → Schizoid PD (indifference + restricted affect, no odd cognition). Stem: "A woman has no close friends, dresses oddly, believes she can sense others' thoughts, and feels passersby are talking about her, yet has never had a sustained psychotic episode." → Schizotypal PD (magical thinking + ideas of reference + eccentricity, attenuated, on the spectrum). Stem: "A man is socially isolated and longs for friendship but avoids people because he is terrified of being criticised or rejected." → Avoidant PD (Cluster C) , NOT schizoid (he wants closeness). Stem: "Which Cluster A disorder is classified within the schizophrenia spectrum in ICD?" → Schizotypal (ICD-10 F21 "Schizotypal Disorder," not a PD in ICD). Trap: the discriminator is odd beliefs / perceptual distortions . No odd beliefs + emotionally cold + happy alone = schizoid. Odd beliefs + social anxiety + eccentric = schizotypal. Schizotypal is NOT schizophrenia (no frank, sustained psychosis) but IS on its spectrum ; schizoid is not . Don't confuse schizoid (a personality disorder, "doesn't want people") with schizophrenia's negative symptoms (which arise within a psychotic illness) or with avoidant PD (Cluster C, wants closeness but fears rejection). Lock the exact answer once you send Q31's full wording/options. Trap (ideas vs delusions of reference): schizotypal has ideas of reference (a self-conscious hunch that events refer to oneself, reality-testing partly intact). A fixed, unshakeable delusion of reference points to a psychotic disorder, not a personality disorder. Trap (paranoid PD vs paranoid schizophrenia / delusional disorder): Paranoid PD = pervasive trait suspiciousness, no fixed delusion. A discrete fixed persecutory belief = delusional disorder ; suspiciousness inside an active psychosis = schizophrenia. Trait vs delusion vs psychosis. Hook: "Schiz oid = v oid of desire for people, no weird beliefs (cold). Schizo typal = typ ically weird (magical thinking, ideas of reference) → on the spectrum. Para noid = on para de against everyone (distrust)." And: Avoidant = " avoids but aches for closeness" (Cluster C), unlike schizoid who simply doesn't care. That's the gap closer — Part A (PYQ audit, 10 clusters) + Part B (today's NIMHANS paper, 16 clusters). Lead line + trap box per cluster is the fast read; the tables are the "which one is it" reference. Every recalled paper topic (1–18, 28–31) is folded in; items 19–27 weren't recalled. Good luck. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · High-Yield Gap Closer · built 2026-05-30 from the PYQ coverage audit

title: Effects, Phenomena, Theories & Originators
text: Effects, Phenomena, Theories & Originators One consolidated lookup for every named effect, phenomenon, illusion, theory, complex and the people behind them. The five old sweeps overlapped heavily (an "effect" carries an originator; a theory carries a theorist), so each item now lives in exactly one entry: the definition, who coined it, the classic study, and the confusable lookalike, together. Drill it both directions: cover the "Who" column and name the person; cover the description and name the term. High-yield NIMHANS / MET ask this two ways. (1) Name the "____ effect / theory / complex" and ask who proposed it (answer = a person). (2) Describe a scene/finding with no name and ask you to name it (answer = the effect/theory). Almost every trap is a same-family lookalike (halo↔horn, Pygmalion↔Golem, placebo↔nocebo, James-Lange↔Cannon-Bard, McCall's T↔Student's t). Always learn each item with its twin. In this reference Named effects (grouped) Phenomena, illusions, biases & clinical signs Theories & models (by domain) Named complexes & syndromes Who originated what — theorists Psychometrics, statistics & standard scores 1. Named effects Every named "____ effect," its originator, and the one-line hook. Grouped by domain so the good-twin / bad-twin pairs sit together. 1.1 Memory & learning effects Effect Who What it is Zeigarnik effect Bluma Zeigarnik Interrupted / unfinished tasks are remembered better than completed ones. Von Restorff (isolation) effect Hedwig von Restorff The odd-one-out item in a list stands out and is recalled best. Serial position effect Ebbinghaus (named by Murdock) First + last items in a list recalled best (= primacy + recency together). Primacy effect — First items recalled well (rehearsed into long-term store). Recency effect — Last items recalled well (still in short-term store). A delay/distractor kills recency, not primacy. Spacing (distributed practice) effect Ebbinghaus Spread-out study beats cramming for long-term retention. Testing effect — Retrieving (self-testing) cements memory better than re-reading. Generation effect Slamecka & Graf Info you generate yourself is remembered better than info you just read. Self-reference effect Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker Material related to yourself is encoded and recalled better. Misinformation effect Elizabeth Loftus Post-event misleading info distorts the original memory (eyewitness work). Picture superiority effect Allan Paivio (dual-coding) Pictures are remembered better than words. Encoding-specificity / context effect Tulving & Thomson Recall is best when retrieval cues match the encoding context (state/context-dependent memory). Levels-of-processing effect Craik & Lockhart Deeper (semantic) processing → better memory than shallow (visual/acoustic). Trap Remove the delay/distractor and it's the recency end that vanishes (STM decays); primacy survives. Zeigarnik = unfinished remembered; von Restorff = distinctive remembered — don't merge them. 1.2 Attention & perception effects Effect Who What it is Stroop effect J. Ridley Stroop Slower to name ink colour when the word spells a different colour (automatic reading interferes). Cocktail-party effect Colin Cherry Selective attention to one voice in a crowd, yet you still catch your own name. McGurk effect McGurk & MacDonald What you see the mouth do changes what you hear (audio-visual speech fusion). Ventriloquist effect — Sound is mislocated toward a plausible visual source. Troxler effect (fading) Ignaz Troxler Fixate steadily and unchanging peripheral stimuli fade from awareness. Motion aftereffect (waterfall illusion) — After staring at motion, a static scene appears to drift the opposite way. Bouba/kiki effect Köhler (later Ramachandran) People map "bouba" to round shapes, "kiki" to spiky ones (sound symbolism). Tetris effect — Heavy repeated activity intrudes into imagery/dreams. Trap The phi phenomenon and autokinetic phenomenon are labelled "phenomena," not "effects" — they live in §2.1. Same content, the label decides where the examiner files it. 1.3 Social & expectancy effects Effect Who What it is Halo effect Edward Thorndike One good trait (e.g. looks) bleeds into an overall positive judgement. Horn(s) effect — The negative mirror of halo: one bad trait darkens the whole impression. Pygmalion (Rosenthal) effect Rosenthal & Jacobson High teacher/leader expectations → the person actually performs better (self-fulfilling prophecy). Golem effect — Low expectations → worse performance (the dark twin of Pygmalion). Hawthorne effect Elton Mayo (Western Electric studies) People change behaviour because they know they're being observed. John Henry effect Saretsky A control group tries extra hard because it knows it's the comparison (a research artefact). Mere-exposure effect Robert Zajonc Repeated exposure alone increases liking (also a persuasion lever: familiarity breeds liking). Bystander effect Latané & Darley More onlookers → less likely any one helps (diffusion of responsibility). After Kitty Genovese. 5-step decision model: notice → interpret → take responsibility → know how → act. (Theory form in §3.6.) Ringelmann effect Max Ringelmann Per-person effort drops as group size grows (precursor to social loafing). Pratfall effect Elliot Aronson A competent person becomes more likeable after a small blunder. Spotlight effect Thomas Gilovich Overestimating how much others notice you. False-consensus effect Lee Ross Overestimating how many people share your views/choices. Lake Wobegon / above-average effect — Most people rate themselves above average (illusory superiority). Cheerleader effect — Faces look more attractive in a group than alone. Overjustification effect Lepper, Greene & Nisbett Paying for an already-enjoyed activity kills the intrinsic motivation. Boomerang effect Hovland tradition (akin to Brehm) Persuasion backfires, shifting the attitude the opposite way (cousin of reactance, §3.6). Trap Same-study, different name: Pygmalion = Rosenthal & Jacobson

title: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options
text: Lookalikes — telling two close terms apart on the options For when plain definitions aren't enough and the trap is a near-identical distractor. Each block is one confusable pair: what's the same (why both look right), what differs (line by line), and the one tell — the single thing in the stem that splits them. Read the tell, not the whole block, on exam day. Built 2026-05-25. Effects Phenomena Theories Theorists Social Psych Cognitive Lookalikes How to use it. The examiner picks two real, correct-sounding terms and bets you can't split them. Don't re-derive both definitions. Find the tell word in the stem (added vs removed? up vs down? before vs after? thought vs act?) and the option falls out. These are the pairs that actually bleed marks on MET/NIMHANS. Jump to: 1. Learning & conditioning 2. Developmental 3. Sensation & perception 4. Memory & cognition 5. Stats & research 6. Abnormal / clinical 7. Defense mechanisms 8. Therapy 9. Social 10. Intelligence 1. Learning & conditioning Classical conditioning vs Operant conditioning Same: both are associative learning; both show acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation and discrimination. Classical (Pavlov) Operant (Skinner) Behaviour Involuntary, reflexive (salivation, fear) Voluntary, emitted (lever press) Association Stimulus → stimulus (CS–US) Behaviour → consequence (response–reinforcer) Learner Passive, responds to a cue Active, operates on the environment Reinforcer timing Comes before/with the response Comes after the response The tell: Is the behaviour automatic and triggered by a cue that comes first (classical), or voluntary and shaped by what happens after (operant)? Any "reward / consequence / punishment" in the stem → operant. Negative reinforcement vs Punishment Same: both are operant procedures and both usually involve an aversive/unpleasant stimulus, so they read alike. Negative reinforcement Punishment Effect on behaviour Increases it Decreases it What happens Removes an aversive stimulus (take painkiller → pain gone) Adds aversive (positive) or removes pleasant (negative) "Negative" means Subtraction, not "bad" — The tell: Did the behaviour go up or down ? Up = reinforcement (negative = the bad thing was taken away ). Down = punishment. "Negative" is about removal, never about being unpleasant. Positive punishment vs Negative punishment Same: both decrease a behaviour. Positive punishment Negative punishment Operation Add something aversive (scolding, spanking) Remove something pleasant (take phone, time-out, fine) Other name — Response cost / omission The tell: Positive = something was added ; negative = something was taken away . Both still reduce the behaviour, so judge by add vs subtract, not by good vs bad. Primary reinforcer vs Secondary reinforcer Same: both strengthen behaviour when they follow it. Primary Secondary (conditioned) Why it reinforces Innately satisfies a biological need (food, water, sex, warmth) Learned value through association Learning needed? No Yes (money, tokens, praise, grades) The tell: Does it satisfy a body need directly (primary) or only because you learned it stands for something else (secondary)? Money is the classic secondary reinforcer. Shaping vs Chaining Same: both build complex operant behaviour using reinforcement. Shaping Chaining What's reinforced Successive approximations to one target behaviour Linking a sequence of already-learned behaviours Picture it Refining one act closer and closer Step 1 → step 2 → step 3 as a chain The tell: One behaviour polished step-by-step (shaping) vs several separate behaviours joined in order (chaining). Stimulus generalisation vs Stimulus discrimination Same: both describe how a conditioned response transfers (or doesn't) across stimuli. Generalisation Discrimination Response to similar cues Yes — spreads to stimuli like the CS No — only the exact CS triggers it Little Albert Feared all furry white things Would fear only the rat The tell: Response spreads to lookalikes (generalisation) vs narrows to one exact cue (discrimination). 2. Developmental Assimilation vs Accommodation (Piaget) Same: the twin processes of adaptation ; both are how a schema deals with new information. Assimilation Accommodation Schema Stays the same — new info forced into it Changes / a new one is created to fit reality Example Calls a whale a "fish" Learns a whale is a mammal, makes a new category The tell: Did the existing schema stay put (assimilation) or did it have to change (accommodation)? If the child updated their mental category, it's accommodation. Piaget vs Vygotsky Same: both constructivists; both say the child actively builds knowledge rather than passively absorbing it. Piaget Vygotsky Engine of development The individual child exploring; cognition leads language Social/cultural interaction; language leads cognition Signature terms Stages, schema, assimilation/accommodation, egocentrism ZPD, scaffolding, More Knowledgeable Other, private speech The tell: Is the driver the child alone (Piaget) or a guiding social other / ZPD (Vygotsky)? Any "scaffolding" or "zone of proximal development" → Vygotsky. 3. Sensation & perception Sensation vs Perception Same: both are stages of taking in stimulus information. Sensation Perception What it is Raw detection by sense organs + transduction Brain's organisation & interpretation of it Direction Bottom-up (data in) Top-down (meaning added) The tell: Detecting the raw signal at the receptor (sensation) vs making sense of / recognising it (perception). Interpretation, meaning, recognition → perception. Absolute threshold vs Difference threshold (JND) Same: both are psychophysics thresholds (Weber/Fechner). Absolute threshold Difference threshold (JND) Detects Minimum intensity to detect a stimulus 50% of the time Smallest detectable change between two stimuli Law — Weber's law: JND is a constant proportion The tell: Detecting that one stimulus is present (absolute) vs detecting a difference between two

title: The Textbook — Everything in One Page
text: The Textbook — Everything in One Page Your single self-contained source. Built 2026-05-22, the night before MET. This is the one page. Read it top to bottom and you have read everything. Every list, definition, table, trap box and concept you have ever been given is inlined here, organised by your 8 exam sections, plus a §9 rapid-recall sweep (the easily-forgotten names/durations and the general-psych foundations) at the end, so it reads like your own textbook. There are no links out to other pages, nothing to chase, all the content lives right here. Study from this page only tonight. Sections are folded so it isn't a wall of text: tap any one to open it, or hit Expand all to read straight through. Jump to ★ Your mock misses, fixed ★C. Common-section concept pack 1. Biopsychology / Neuro 2. Developmental 3. Abnormal 4. Assessment / Tests 5. Psychotherapy / Learning / Ethics 6. Research / Biostats 7. Language 8. Social / Memory / Acts / Founders 9. Rapid Recall (easily forgotten + general psych) Exam-day rules Expand all Collapse all Tap a section to open it. Everything is still here, just folded away. ★ Your mock misses, fixed here Every question you got wrong, guessed, or flagged on the real NIMHANS 2024 PYQ mock (91.25/100) maps to a block below. If you only have an hour, read these rows, then read the red trap boxes. What tripped you The fix Section WAIS scaled score of 10 = ?
