Exactly average, 50th percentile (subtest mean 10, SD 3) Biostats WAIS-IV core subtest NOT in WISC-V Letter-Number Sequencing (WAIS-IV WMI core; WISC-V uses Picture Span instead) Assessment IQ test = which kind of test? Ability test (maximum performance). Not power, not speed. Assessment Bystander effect explained by… Diffusion of responsibility + pluralistic ignorance Social Mania NOT first-line drug Fluoxetine (an SSRI; can trigger a manic switch) Neuro BPD feature NOT in NPD Pervasive instability of relationships + self-image Abnormal "Real relationship" + UPR over "alliance" Person-centred (Rogers) Therapy Kohut / self-psychology / "mirroring" Failure of parental mirroring → grandiosity; mirroring + idealizing failure → fragmented self Therapy What is ataxia vs apraxia? Ataxia = loss of coordination/balance ; apraxia = can't sequence learned movements Neuro Who is Kitty Genovese? 1964 NYC murder, allegedly many witnesses, none helped → launched bystander research Social Type D personality? Negative affectivity + social inhibition ; poor cardiac prognosis Abnormal Escape vs avoidance learning Escape terminates an aversive stimulus already on; avoidance prevents its onset Therapy Object relations meaning Internalised mental representations of self and others Therapy Memory: what/where/when of an event Episodic memory Memory Spearman → factor analysis, Wundt → ? Introspection (structuralism's method) Founders MHCA 2017 + minors Minor can appoint a nominated representative; views considered age-appropriately Acts OR / RR of 1 No association. >1 increased risk, <1 protective Biostats NNT 1 / ARR. Lower NNT = better drug Biostats "Data" singular or plural? Plural in formal use ("data are…"); datum is singular Language ★C. Common-Section Concept Pack high-yield general psych · the foundations · the bits that quietly cost marks This is the section that is bleeding your marks. The subject blocks above are your strong ground; the common section is general psychology, and it punishes shaky foundations and confusable pairs more than raw facts. So this pack is built differently: every block ends in the exact distinction the examiner uses to separate the two options that look identical. Read it for the contrasts, not the trivia. If you can run the cover-and-test set at the very end (C.11) clean, the common section stops costing you. C.1 The schools of psychology (the "isms"), in order Almost every general paper has one "who founded / what method / which school" item. Learn them as a story: each school is a reaction to the one before it. School Core claim Method Key names Structuralism Break consciousness into its basic elements (sensations, feelings) Introspection Wundt (first lab, 1879), Titchener Functionalism Why does the mind do what it does; its purpose and adaptation Observation, applied focus William James, Dewey, Angell Gestalt The whole is different from the sum of its parts; perception is organised Phenomenology Wertheimer, Koffka, Köhler Psychoanalysis Behaviour is driven by the unconscious and early conflict Free association, dream analysis, case study Freud, later Jung, Adler Behaviourism Study only observable behaviour; the mind is a black box Controlled experiment, conditioning Watson, Pavlov, Skinner, Thorndike Humanistic People are growth-oriented and free; the "third force" Phenomenology, client report Maslow, Rogers Cognitive Mind as an information processor; mental processes are real and studiable Experiment, modelling, reaction time Neisser (coined it, 1967), Miller, Broadbent Biological Behaviour reduces to brain, neurochemistry, genes Lesion, imaging, twin studies Sperry, Hebb Evolutionary Behaviour was selected because it aided survival/reproduction Cross-species, adaptationist reasoning Buss, Tooby & Cosmides Positive Study strengths, well-being and flourishing, not just pathology Empirical, intervention trials Seligman, Csikszentmihalyi TRAP: Wundt = structuralism + introspection (the first lab). James = functionalism . Neisser = cognitive . Watson named behaviourism but Wundt is "father of experimental psychology"; Lewin is "father of social psychology"; Wundt is NOT a functionalist. Gestalt is a perception school, not a therapy (do not confuse it with Perls' Gestalt therapy ). C.2 Sensation vs perception, and psychophysics Sensation = the raw signal a receptor sends up (bottom-up). Perception = the brain organising and interpreting it (adds top-down expectation, context, schema). Same retinal image, two perceptions = perception > sensation. Absolute threshold: the smallest intensity detectable 50% of the time. Difference threshold = JND (just noticeable difference): the smallest change you can detect 50% of the time. Sensory adaptation: constant unchanging stimulus, receptors stop responding (you stop feeling your watch). Law What it says The hook Weber's law The JND is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, not a fixed amount Add 1 candle to 1, you notice; add 1 to 100, you do not Fechner's law Sensation grows with the logarithm of stimulus intensity Built psychophysics on Weber's finding Stevens' power law Sensation is a power function of intensity (fits more senses than Fechner) The modern refinement Signal Detection Theory: detection is not just sensitivity, it is a decision. Four outcomes: Hit (signal there, said yes), Miss (signal there, said no), False alarm (no signal, said yes), Correct rejection (no signal, said no). d′ = true sensitivity; the criterion (β) = how willing you are to say "yes". A tired or motivated observer shifts criterion, not sensitivity. TRAP: Weber = constant ratio (JND). Fechner = log . Do not say Weber gives a fixed amount. SDT separates sensitivity (d′) from response bias (criterion); a question about "willingness to report" is about the criterion, not d′. C.3 Gestalt organisation, constancies, depth cues Gestalt grouping laws: figure-ground, proximity (near things group), similarity (alike things group), closure (fill the gap), continuity / good continuation (smooth lines), common fate (things moving together group), Prägnanz (we see the simplest possible form). The umbrella principle is Prägnanz, "the law of good figure". Perceptual constancies: size, shape, colour, brightness stay stable even as the retinal image changes. A door is still rectangular when open (shape constancy). Depth cues: binocular = retinal disparity + convergence (need both eyes, work near). Monocular = relative size, interposition/overlap, linear perspective, texture gradient, aerial perspective, motion parallax, light & shadow (work with one eye, mostly for distance). TRAP: Retinal disparity and convergence are the only two binocular cues; everything else is monocular. Motion parallax is monocular even though it sounds complex. C.4 Learning: the distinctions that quietly cost marks Classical (Pavlov) Operant (Skinner) What is learned An association between two stimuli An association between behaviour and its consequence Behaviour is Reflexive, involuntary (elicited) Voluntary (emitted) Order Stimulus comes before the response Consequence comes after the response Example Dog salivates to a bell Rat presses a lever for food Classical terms: UCS → UCR (unlearned); the NS becomes the CS when paired, producing the CR . Acquisition (learning), extinction (CS alone, CR fades), spontaneous recovery (the CR returns after a rest), generalisation (similar stimuli also trigger it), discrimination (only the exact CS does). Little Albert = generalised fear; Garcia effect = one-trial taste aversion (biological preparedness). The four operant contingencies (the classic trap): "Positive" = add a stimulus, "Negative" = remove one. "Reinforcement" = behaviour increases , "Punishment" = behaviour decreases . Increases behaviour (reinforcement) Decreases behaviour (punishment) Add stimulus (positive) Positive reinforcement (give a treat) Positive punishment (give a scolding) Remove stimulus (negative) Negative reinforcement (stop the alarm by buckling up) Negative punishment / omission (take away the phone) TRAP (this is the one people miss): Negative reinforcement is NOT punishment. It removes something unpleasant to increase a behaviour. Taking aspirin to end a headache is negatively reinforced. Punishment always decreases behaviour. Reinforcement schedule Pattern Response feature Fixed ratio (FR) Reward after a set number of responses High rate, short post-reward pause Variable ratio (VR) Reward after an unpredictable number Highest, steadiest rate; most resistant to extinction (gambling) Fixed interval (FI) Reward for the first response after a set time Scalloped (work speeds up near the deadline) Variable interval (VI) Reward after an unpredictable time Slow, steady (checking for a text) Other learning terms: Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations. Primary reinforcer = innately satisfying (food, water); secondary = learned value (money, tokens). Premack principle = a high-frequency behaviour reinforces a low-frequency one ("eat your veggies, then dessert"). Continuous reinforcement learns fastest; partial reinforcement resists extinction best (the partial-reinforcement effect). TRAP: "Most resistant to extinction" = variable ratio . "Fastest acquisition" = continuous . Do not swap those two questions. C.5 Motivation Theory Core idea Instinct Behaviour is innate and species-typical (early, now largely rejected as a full account) Drive-reduction (Hull) A need creates a drive (tension); behaviour reduces it to restore homeostasis Arousal / optimal level We seek an optimum level of arousal, not zero (explains curiosity); see Yerkes-Dodson Incentive External rewards pull behaviour (drives push, incentives pull) Maslow's hierarchy Physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation; lower needs first Self-determination (Deci & Ryan) Three innate needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness McClelland Acquired needs: achievement (nAch), affiliation, power Yerkes-Dodson law: performance is an inverted-U of arousal. The optimum is lower for difficult/complex tasks and higher for simple/well-learned ones. TRAP: Intrinsic motivation = the activity itself is the reward; extrinsic = an outside reward. The overjustification effect: paying someone for something they already enjoy can reduce the intrinsic motivation. Drives push (internal need), incentives pull (external goal). C.6 Emotion: the theories side by side Every emotion question turns on the order of three events: the stimulus, the bodily arousal, and the felt emotion. Learn the sequence each theory claims. Theory The sequence it claims James-Lange Stimulus → bodily arousal → emotion. "We are afraid because we tremble." Emotion follows the body. Cannon-Bard Stimulus → arousal AND emotion at the same time (thalamus routes to both). Body and feeling are simultaneous, not causal. Schachter-Singer two-factor Stimulus → arousal → cognitive label of that arousal → emotion. Same arousal, different label, different emotion (the adrenaline study). Lazarus appraisal Stimulus → cognitive appraisal comes first → arousal + emotion. Thinking precedes feeling. Facial feedback The face itself feeds emotion: holding a smile can lift mood. TRAP: James-Lange = body first , then emotion. Cannon-Bard = simultaneous . Schachter-Singer adds a cognitive label to arousal. Lazarus puts appraisal first . A stem about "interpreting your racing heart as either fear or excitement" is Schachter-Singer. C.7 Memory Multi-store (Atkinson-Shiffrin): sensory register (iconic ~0.5 s, echoic ~2–4 s) → short-term (~7±2 items, ~15–30 s, lost by displacement/decay) → long-term (effectively unlimited). Rehearsal moves STM → LTM. Working memory (Baddeley): the central executive directs three slaves: the phonological loop (verbal), the visuospatial sketchpad (visual/spatial), and the episodic buffer (binds + links to LTM). This replaced the passive STM "box". LTM types: Explicit/declarative (conscious) splits into episodic (events, what/where/when) and semantic (facts). Implicit/non-declarative includes procedural (skills), priming, and conditioning. Levels of processing (Craik & Lockhart): deeper, semantic processing yields better recall than shallow (visual/phonemic) processing. Serial position: first items recalled well ( primacy , rehearsed into LTM) and last items recalled well ( recency , still in STM). A delay before recall wipes recency but not primacy. Forgetting: decay (trace fades), interference , cue-dependent (encoding-specificity, state- and context-dependent recall), motivated forgetting (repression). Ebbinghaus = the forgetting curve (steep then levels off). Memory is reconstructive: Bartlett's schemas ("War of the Ghosts"), Loftus's misinformation effect (leading questions reshape eyewitness memory). TRAP: Proactive interference = old learning blocks new ("pro" = forward, old pushes ahead). Retroactive = new learning blocks old ("retro" = backward). Recall (produce it) is harder than recognition (pick it out). Episodic = tied to a time and place; semantic = a free-floating fact. C.8 Intelligence and IQ scoring Theory Claim Spearman A general factor g underlies all abilities, plus task-specific s Thurstone 7 independent primary mental abilities, no single g Cattell-Horn Fluid (reasoning on novel problems, declines with age) vs crystallised (accumulated knowledge, holds/rises) Gardner 8 multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical-math, spatial, musical, bodily, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalist) Sternberg Triarchic: analytical, creative, practical Salovey & Mayer / Goleman Emotional intelligence (the model / the popularisation) Scoring foundations: Ratio IQ = (mental age / chronological age) × 100 (old Stanford-Binet). Deviation IQ (Wechsler) = mean 100, SD 15 ; it compares you to your age peers. A WAIS subtest scaled score has mean 10, SD 3 , so a 10 is exactly average (50th percentile). The Flynn effect = average IQ scores rose across the 20th century, so norms need re-standardising. TRAP: Full-scale IQ mean 100 SD 15; scaled subtest mean 10 SD 3. A scaled score of 10 = average, NOT low. Fluid intelligence falls with age; crystallised does not. C.9 Statistics & research the common section quietly tests Central tendency: mean (pulled toward the tail by skew/outliers), median (robust, best for skewed income-type data), mode (the only one usable for nominal data). In a positive (right) skew the order is mode < median < mean; in a negative skew it reverses. The mean is dragged toward the longer tail. Normal curve: symmetrical, mean = median = mode. 68 / 95 / 99.7 of cases fall within 1 / 2 / 3 SD. A z-score = how many SDs a value sits from the mean. Correlation: r ranges −1 to +1 ; the sign is direction, the absolute value is strength. r = 0 means no linear relationship. r² (coefficient of determination) = proportion of variance shared. Correlation does not equal causation (third-variable, directionality problems). Reliability (consistency) vs validity (accuracy). Reliability types: test-retest, inter-rater, internal consistency (Cronbach's α, split-half). Validity types: content, construct, criterion (concurrent + predictive). A test can be reliable but not valid (a consistent bathroom scale that reads 5 kg heavy). It cannot be valid without being reliable. Levels of measurement (NOIR): Nominal (categories), Ordinal (ranked), Interval (equal gaps, no true zero, e.g. Celsius/IQ), Ratio (true zero, e.g. weight, reaction time). Variables: the independent variable is manipulated; the dependent variable is measured. A confound varies with the IV and offers a rival explanation. Random assignment (to groups) controls confounds; random sampling gives generalisability. They are not the same thing. TRAP: Reliable ≠ valid: consistency is not accuracy. In a positively skewed distribution the mean is the highest of the three averages (pulled right). Random assignment ≠ random sampling . Interval has no true zero; ratio does. C.10 Developmental spine (compact) Piaget stage Age Hallmark Sensorimotor 0–2 Object permanence develops Preoperational 2–7 Symbols, egocentrism, no conservation Concrete operational 7–11 Conservation, reversibility, logic on concrete things Formal operational 11+ Abstract and hypothetical reasoning Erikson (8 crises): trust v mistrust → autonomy v shame → initiative v guilt → industry v inferiority → identity v role confusion (adolescence) → intimacy v isolation → generativity v stagnation → integrity v despair. Kohlberg: Preconventional (punishment/reward) → Conventional (social approval/law-and-order) → Postconventional (social contract/universal ethics). Attachment (Ainsworth Strange Situation): secure; insecure-avoidant; insecure-resistant/ambivalent; (Main & Solomon) disorganised. Harlow's monkeys = contact comfort over food; Bowlby = the attachment behavioural system + monotropy. TRAP: Piaget's assimilation = fit new info into an existing schema; accommodation = change the schema to fit new info. Object permanence = sensorimotor ; conservation = concrete operational . Vygotsky stresses the social/ZPD, Piaget the individual constructor. C.11 Cover-and-test: the confusable pairs that quietly cost marks This is the highest-yield drill in the pack. Cover the right column. If you can give the distinction for every row without peeking, the common section is no longer your weak point. Confusable pair The one-line distinction Sensation vs perception Sensation = raw detection (bottom-up); perception = interpretation (adds top-down) Negative reinforcement vs punishment Neg. reinforcement increases behaviour by removing something bad; punishment decreases behaviour Positive vs negative (in conditioning) Positive = add a stimulus; negative = remove one. Nothing to do with good/bad Classical vs operant Classical = involuntary, stimulus before response; operant = voluntary, consequence after response Proactive vs retroactive interference Proactive = old blocks new; retroactive = new blocks old Recall vs recognition Recall = produce it from scratch (harder); recognition = identify the right one (easier) Assimilation vs accommodation Assimilate = bend the world to the schema; accommodate = bend the schema to the world Reliability vs validity Reliability = consistent; validity = measures what it claims. Reliable need not be valid Random sampling vs random assignment Sampling = who gets in the study (generalisability); assignment = which group they go to (controls confounds) Independent vs dependent variable IV = manipulated cause; DV = measured effect Mean vs median in skew The mean chases the tail; the median resists it. Use median for skewed data Fluid vs crystallised intelligence Fluid = reason on the novel (falls with age); crystallised = stored knowledge (holds) Ratio vs deviation IQ Ratio = MA/CA×100 (old); deviation = SD-based comparison to age peers (mean 100, SD 15) James-Lange vs Cannon-Bard James-Lange = body first then emotion; Cannon-Bard = both at once Intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation Intrinsic = the act rewards itself; extrinsic = an outside reward. Beware the overjustification effect Drive vs incentive Drives push from an internal need; incentives pull from an external goal Episodic vs semantic memory Episodic = tied to a time/place; semantic = a free-standing fact Weber vs Fechner Weber = JND is a constant ratio; Fechner = sensation grows with the log of intensity Binocular vs monocular depth cues Binocular = disparity + convergence (two eyes); everything else, incl. motion parallax, is monocular Conformity vs obedience Conformity (Asch) = matching peers; obedience (Milgram) = following an authority's order g vs s (Spearman) g = the general factor across all tasks; s = ability specific to one task Primacy vs recency Primacy = early items (into LTM via rehearsal); recency = last items (still in STM, wiped by delay) If you run C.11 clean, you have closed the gap. These pairs are exactly the "looks like two right answers" items that the common section uses to separate the 70s from the 90s. 1. Biopsychology & Neuropsychology MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 15 Q 1.1 The neuron and glia Dendrites receive input (spines multiply surface area). Soma integrates input. Axon hillock = trigger zone, decides if threshold is reached. Axon conducts the AP. Axon terminals release neurotransmitter. Neuron types: Sensory (afferent, periphery → CNS, pseudounipolar); Motor (efferent, CNS → muscle/gland, multipolar); Interneurons (local CNS processing, most common). Glial cell Location Function Oligodendrocyte CNS Myelinates many axons (one cell, many segments) Schwann cell PNS Myelinates one axon segment per cell Astrocyte CNS Blood-brain barrier, K+ buffering, NT recycling Microglia CNS Immune defence, phagocytosis Ependymal cell Ventricles Produces and circulates CSF Satellite cell PNS ganglia Supports cell bodies in PNS TRAP: CNS myelination = oligodendrocyte. PNS myelination = Schwann cell. 1.2 The action potential (the single most testable neurophysiology topic) An AP is a ~1 ms electrical pulse travelling down the axon. The whole story is " Na+ in, K+ out ": Na+ rushing in depolarises; K+ leaving repolarises. Resting membrane potential ~ −70 mV. Set by K+ leak channels (membrane ~50× more permeable to K+), NOT by the Na/K pump. Threshold ~ −55 mV. Na/K pump: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP. Electrogenic. Maintains the gradient but does not set RMP. Phase 1 Depolarisation: voltage-gated Na+ channels open → Na+ in → spike to ~ +30 mV. Phase 2 Repolarisation: Na+ channels inactivate, voltage-gated K+ channels open (slower) → K+ out. Phase 3 Hyperpolarisation: K+ channels stay open briefly → undershoot below −70 mV. Phase 4 Return: K+ channels close, Na/K pump restores ions. Ion concentrations: "K is in, Na is out, Cl is out, Ca is way out." Equilibrium potentials: K+ −90 mV, Na+ +60 mV, Cl− −65 mV, Ca²⁺ +120 mV. All-or-none law: once threshold is reached the AP fires at constant amplitude; stimulus intensity is coded by frequency , not amplitude. Refractory periods: Absolute = Na+ channels inactivated, no stimulus however strong can fire another AP (ensures one-way propagation). Relative = membrane hyperpolarised (K+ still open), a stronger stimulus can fire one. TRAP: Inactivated ≠ closed. The Na+ channel has 3 states: closed (resting), open (during AP), inactivated (after, "ball and chain" blocks the pore). Resets only after repolarisation. Propagation: continuous (unmyelinated C fibres, 0.5–2 m/s) vs saltatory (myelinated, AP jumps between Nodes of Ranvier, up to 120 m/s in A-alpha). Conduction velocity rises with myelination > axon diameter > temperature. Demyelination (MS, Guillain-Barré) slows/blocks conduction. Synaptic transmission: AP arrives → voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open, Ca²⁺ enters → vesicles fuse (SNARE proteins, synaptotagmin = Ca²⁺ sensor) → NT released → binds postsynaptic receptors → EPSP (Na+/Ca²⁺ in, depolarising) or IPSP (Cl− in or K+ out, hyperpolarising) → cleared by reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, or diffusion. Summation (spatial + temporal) at the axon hillock decides if a new AP fires. TRAP: Ca²⁺ is the trigger ion for NT release at the terminal. Without Ca²⁺ entry, no transmitter is released. 1.3 Neurotransmitters (the 7 families) NT Class / made from Cleared by Clinical link Acetylcholine (ACh) Choline + acetyl-CoA Acetylcholinesterase Low in Alzheimer's; myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR); NMJ Dopamine Catecholamine (Tyrosine → DOPA → DA) Reuptake, MAO, COMT ↑ mesolimbic = +ve schizophrenia. Developmental Psychology MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 10 Q 2.1 Foundational principles Cephalocaudal (head → toe) · Proximodistal (centre → periphery). Critical period = rigid biological window, lost if missed (Lorenz imprinting). Sensitive period = optimal but flexible (language acquisition). Psychological Assessment & Tests MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 10 Q The whole map: a psychological test is a measuring instrument that must be (a) consistent = reliability and (b) accurate = validity . Everything else is a way to estimate one of those, interpret scores against norms, or an example of a real test. 4.1 Item analysis Difficulty index p = proportion who got the item right (0–1). Sweet spot 0.50 for free-response, ~0.625 for a 4-option MCQ (halfway between guessing 0.25 and ceiling). p > 0.80 too easy, < 0.20 too hard. Discrimination index D = p(top 27%) − p(bottom 27%), range −1 to +1. D > 0.40 good. Negative D = mis-keyed/ambiguous item, discard immediately. 4.2 Reliability (consistency) Classical test theory: Observed = True + Error. Reliability = proportion of variance that is true. Test-retest (across time; standard window 2–4 wks). Parallel forms (across forms). Split-half + Spearman-Brown correction (r_full = 2·r_half / (1 + r_half)); Cronbach α (≥0.7 acceptable, ≥0.8 good) = mean of all possible split-halves; KR-20 for dichotomous (0/1) items. Inter-rater: Cohen κ (categorical, Landis & Koch: 0.61–0.80 substantial, 0.81+ almost perfect), ICC (continuous). SEM = SD·√(1 − r_xx). Higher reliability → smaller SEM → tighter confidence band around a score. TRAP: Cronbach α is NOT a measure of unidimensionality — a test can have high α and still measure two constructs. And κ is NOT internal consistency. 4.3 Validity (accuracy) Content: covers the domain (expert panels, Lawshe's CVR). Face validity = looks valid to a layperson, the weakest form. Criterion: Concurrent (criterion now) vs Predictive = Postponed (criterion later). Construct: convergent (correlates with similar) + discriminant (not with unrelated) + nomological network. Campbell & Fiske's multitrait-multimethod matrix (MTMM, 1959). Validity ceiling: max validity = √(reliability). Unreliable tests cannot be strongly valid. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. 4.4 Test classification Type Means Maximum performance (ability/aptitude/achievement, e.g. IQ) Do your best . There is a right answer Typical performance (personality, interest, attitude) What you usually do. No right answer Power test Hard items, generous time — measures ceiling of ability Speed test Easy items, tight time — measures how fast The exact trap you missed: an IQ test is an ability test (maximum performance), not a power or speed test. Achievement = what you learned (past, WIAT). Aptitude = what you can learn (future, DAT/SAT). Intelligence = general capacity. Norm-referenced (vs peers) vs criterion-referenced (vs absolute standard). Formative (during) vs summative (end). 4.5 Standard scores & norms Standard score = M + (SD × z). Chaining = link existing behaviours (each is the S D for the next; backward chaining preferred clinically). Fading = remove the prompt (extinction removes the reinforcer ). Prompting hierarchy: physical → modelling → gestural → verbal → visual. Extinction: watch for the extinction burst ; extinction suppresses, doesn't erase. Spontaneous recovery proves the memory is intact. Generalization is the default; discrimination is trained by differential reinforcement. Schedules: VR = highest, steadiest rate, most resistant to extinction (gambling). VI = steady moderate (checking phone). FR = post-reinforcement pause then burst (piece-work). FI = scallop (studying before a weekly quiz). Resistance: VR > VI > FR > FI > continuous. Latent learning (Tolman, cognitive map — learning without reinforcement, shown later). Insight learning (Köhler's Sultan, sudden "aha"). Observational learning (Bandura Bobo doll; 4 processes ARRM: Attention → Retention → Reproduction → Motivation; vicarious reinforcement). Habituation vs sensitization (Kandel, Aplysia, non-associative). Escape vs avoidance (your mock guess): Escape = behaviour terminates an aversive stimulus that is already present (turn off a loud alarm). Avoidance = behaviour prevents the aversive stimulus from starting (leave before the alarm). Both are negative reinforcement. 5.8 Ethics in practice Principle (Beauchamp & Childress) One line / in practice Autonomy Respect the client's right to decide — informed consent, right to refuse Beneficence Act for the client's good — choose the treatment most likely to help Non-maleficence "First, do no harm" — withhold harmful/unproven methods, stay within competence Justice Fairness — no discrimination, equitable access Informed consent = disclosure + capacity + voluntariness. Assent = a minor's agreement alongside a parent's consent. Paternalism = overriding a competent person's choice (violates autonomy). Confidentiality = your duty; privacy = the client's right; privileged communication = legal protection in court. Other terms: Fidelity (loyalty), Veracity (truth-telling), Competence, Dual/multiple relationship (boundary violation), Negligence (below standard of care). Confidentiality is NOT absolute — it breaks for risk of serious harm to self/others, suspected child/elder abuse (mandatory reporting), or court order. Tarasoff duty to warn/protect: a credible threat against an identifiable person obliges the therapist to act — non-maleficence/beneficence to a third party overrides confidentiality. The classic swap: beneficence = do good vs non-maleficence = avoid harm . 6. Power = 1 − β (aim ≥ 0.80; rises with larger n, larger effect, larger α, lower variability, one-tailed). p-value = probability of the observed result or more extreme if H0 were true. NOT the probability that H0 is true. p < α → reject H0. 95% CI: if repeated, 95% of intervals would contain the true parameter. Specificity = TN/(TN+FP), rules a condition IN when positive ( SpPin ). PPV/NPV depend on prevalence; likelihood ratios don't. ROC plots sensitivity vs (1−specificity). Language & Communication Skills MET 15 Q · NIMHANS 5 Q · highest fast-marks ratio 7.1 Subject-verb agreement The verb agrees with the subject in number, not the nearest noun. Each, every, either, neither, one, anyone, everyone, nobody → singular ("Each of the participants was given…"). Either/or, neither/nor → verb agrees with the nearer subject ("Neither the patient nor the family members were informed"). "A number of" = plural; "the number of" = singular. None defaults singular in formal writing. "Data are" — data is technically plural (datum singular); treat as plural in exam contexts. Singular-looking: news, mathematics, physics, politics, statistics. Plural-only: scissors, trousers, glasses. 7.2 Voice & conditionals Active → passive: object becomes subject; verb → "be" + past participle. "The committee will announce the results" → "The results will be announced by the committee." Conditional If-clause Main clause Zero (general truths) present present First (real future) present will + base Second (hypothetical) past would + base Third (counterfactual past) past perfect ("Had she taken") would have + past participle Mixed past perfect would + base " Had she taken the medication, she would have recovered sooner" = third conditional (inversion is formal). 7.3 Punctuation & prepositions Restrictive vs non-restrictive clauses: non-restrictive (extra info, removable) → commas + "who"; restrictive (defines which) → no commas, "that". "The patient, who was anxious, refused" (one patient) vs "The patient who was anxious refused" (picks out one of several). Semicolon joins two independent clauses; colon introduces a list/explanation. It's = it is; its = possessive. Prepositions: insist on , depend on, comply with, consist of, refer to, suffer from, object to, accuse of, married to (not with), prefer X to Y, superior/inferior to (not than), discuss (no preposition). "Between you and me ." 7.4 Modifiers, parallelism & common corrections Dangling modifier: "Walking down the street, the building looked tall" (the building isn't walking). Parallelism: "reading, writing, and swimming" (not "to swim"). Like (before a noun) vs as (before a clause). Who (subject) vs whom (object). Less (uncountable) vs fewer (countable). Between (two) vs among (3+). "The reason is that " (not "because"). Predicate adjective follows a linking verb ("The data were inconclusive "). 7.5 Vocabulary, one-word substitutions & idioms Word Meaning / pairing Gregarious Sociable (antonym: reclusive) Ephemeral Lasting briefly (synonym: transient) Ambivalent Mixed feelings (NOT indifferent = no feeling) Garrulous / loquacious / verbose Talkative / wordy Laconic / taciturn / reticent Few words / reserved Sagacious / cogent / pragmatic Wise / convincing / practical Frugal / abstemious Sparing with money / with food & drink Capricious / whimsical / vacillate Unpredictable / playful / waver Egregious / belligerent / obstinate Outstandingly bad / hostile / stubborn Definition Word Fluent in many languages Polyglot Fear of confined / open spaces Claustrophobia / Agoraphobia Hates / loves humanity Misanthrope / Philanthropist Walker in sleep Somnambulist Cure-all medicine Panacea Speech without preparation Extempore Never drinks alcohol Teetotaller Idioms: bury the hatchet (make peace), hit the nail on the head (be right), beat around the bush (avoid the point), bite the bullet (endure), a blessing in disguise, cut corners, burn the midnight oil. Social psych first since that is where the named-experiment questions cluster. Theorist What they actually did · the trap Social psychology Asch Conformity. Line-judgement task: pick which of 3 lines matches a standard. Confederates deliberately gave a wrong answer; about 75% of real subjects conformed at least once, ~33% on average. Conformity is normative (fit in / avoid disapproval), not informational. Trap: Asch = group peer pressure; Milgram = authority . Conformity dropped sharply with one dissenting ally. Milgram Obedience. "Teacher" told by experimenter to shock a "learner" for wrong answers, up to 450V. 65% went to the maximum shock. Showed ordinary people obey a legitimate authority. Trap: obedience = following an authority's order ; conformity (Asch) = matching peers . Zimbardo Stanford Prison Experiment. Students randomly assigned guard/prisoner roles; "guards" turned abusive fast, study stopped after 6 days. Power of the situation/assigned role over personality (deindividuation). Trap: situational, not dispositional. Sherif Robbers Cave / realistic conflict theory. Two boys' camp groups; competition bred hostility, and superordinate goals (shared tasks neither group could solve alone) reduced it. Contact alone was not enough. Tajfel Social identity theory + minimal group paradigm. Even arbitrary grouping (e.g. coin toss) produced in-group favouritism . Identity comes from group membership; basis of prejudice. Festinger Cognitive dissonance + social comparison theory. Festinger & Carlsmith: people paid $1 to lie about a boring task changed their attitude more than those paid $20 (less external justification → more internal change). Trap: the smaller reward causes the bigger attitude shift. Latane & Darley Bystander effect / diffusion of responsibility (Kitty Genovese). More bystanders → less likely any one helps. Steps: notice → interpret as emergency → assume responsibility → help. Lewin "Father of social psychology." Field theory (B = f(P,E): behaviour is a function of person and environment); leadership styles; unfreeze–change–refreeze model of change. Heider Attribution theory + balance theory. We explain behaviour by internal (dispositional) vs external (situational) causes. Related: fundamental attribution error = over-blaming the person, under-weighting the situation. Kelley Covariation model of attribution: we judge cause using consensus, consistency, distinctiveness . Bem Self-perception theory: we infer our own attitudes by observing our own behaviour (the reverse of dissonance). Learning Pavlov Classical conditioning. Neutral stimulus (bell) paired with food (UCS) becomes a conditioned stimulus producing salivation (CR). Terms: acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination. Watson Behaviourism founder. Little Albert: conditioned a baby to fear a white rat (paired with a loud noise); fear generalised to furry things. Thorndike Law of effect (cat puzzle box): responses followed by satisfaction are stamped in. Precursor to operant conditioning. Skinner Operant conditioning. Behaviour shaped by consequences. Reinforcement schedules: variable-ratio gives the highest, most extinction-resistant response rate. Positive/negative reinforcement both increase behaviour; punishment decreases it. Bandura Social learning / Bobo doll: children imitated aggression they observed , no direct reward needed. Also self-efficacy and reciprocal determinism. Tolman Latent learning + cognitive maps (purposive behaviourism). Tolman & Honzik maze: the group given a reward only from day 11 suddenly matched the always-rewarded group, proving they'd learned the maze all along without reinforcement. Behaviour is goal-directed ; animals build a mental "map." Trap: learning ≠ performance. Rotter Social learning theory + locus of control. Behaviour potential = expectancy × reinforcement value . Internal LOC ("I control my outcomes") vs external LOC ("luck/fate/others do"); measured by his I–E Scale . Cognitive bridge between behaviourism and personality. Memory Ebbinghaus Forgetting curve using nonsense syllables; most forgetting happens fast then levels off. Also the spacing effect. Miller "Magic number 7 ± 2" : short-term memory holds about 5–9 chunks. Baddeley Working memory model (4 parts): central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer. Replaced the single STM box. Tulving Long-term memory split: episodic (events) vs semantic (facts) vs procedural (skills). Loftus Misinformation effect: leading questions distort eyewitness memory ("smashed" vs "hit" changed speed estimates). Memory is reconstructive. Bartlett Reconstructive memory + schemas ("War of the Ghosts"): recall is rebuilt to fit existing schemas, not replayed. Development Piaget 4 cognitive stages: sensorimotor (object permanence), preoperational (egocentrism, no conservation), concrete operational (conservation), formal operational (abstract). Assimilation vs accommodation. Vygotsky Sociocultural: learning is social. Zone of proximal development = gap between what a child can do alone vs with help; scaffolding . Erikson 8 psychosocial stages , each a crisis (e.g. trust vs mistrust, identity vs role confusion in adolescence). Spans the whole lifespan. Kohlberg Moral development: 3 levels (pre-conventional, conventional, post-conventional), 6 stages. Trap: Gilligan criticised it as male-biased and added the ethic of care . Bowlby / Ainsworth Attachment. Ainsworth's Strange Situation → secure, anxious-ambivalent, avoidant (+ disorganised). Harlow's monkeys: contact comfort beats food. Personality Freud Psychoanalysis: id–ego–superego; 5 psychosexual stages (oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital); defence mechanisms; unconscious. Jung Analytical psychology: collective unconscious, archetypes, introversion/extraversion. Adler Individual psychology: inferiority complex, striving for superiority, birth order. Eysenck / Cattell / Allport Trait theorists: Eysenck = PEN (3 dims); Cattell = 16 PF ; Allport = cardinal/central/secondary. Big Five (OCEAN) is the dominant model now. Rogers / Maslow Humanistic: Rogers = client-centred, unconditional positive regard, congruence; Maslow = hierarchy of needs → self-actualisation. Intelligence & therapy Spearman Two-factor: general g + specific s ; invented factor analysis. Gardner / Sternberg Gardner = multiple intelligences (8); Sternberg = triarchic (analytical, creative, practical). Binet / Terman / Wechsler Binet = first practical test (mental age); Terman = Stanford-Binet, IQ ratio; Wechsler = WAIS/WISC, deviation IQ (mean 100, SD 15). Beck / Ellis Beck = cognitive triad + CBT; Ellis = REBT , the ABC model. Both target distorted thinking. "purpose/adaptation" → James/functionalism. "whole > parts" → Gestalt. "free will/self-actualisation" → humanistic. 9.7 Motivation & drive Theory Says Maslow's hierarchy Physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualisation . Lower needs first Drive-reduction (Hull) Need → drive → behaviour to restore homeostasis Arousal / Yerkes-Dodson Seek optimal arousal; moderate arousal = best performance (inverted-U); hard tasks need lower arousal Incentive theory Pulled by external rewards (vs pushed by internal drives) Intrinsic vs extrinsic For its own sake vs for a reward. Overjustification effect : paying for an enjoyed task kills intrinsic motivation Self-determination (Deci & Ryan) Three needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness McClelland Need for achievement, affiliation, power 9.8 States of consciousness (sleep one-glance) Item Recall Sleep stages NREM 1→2→3 (deep / slow-wave / delta), then REM (dreaming, paralysis, EEG looks awake) Cycle length ~90 min; REM lengthens toward morning Circadian rhythm ~24 hr clock; suprachiasmatic nucleus + melatonin (pineal) Sleep spindles / K-complexes Hallmark of Stage 2 NREM Delta waves Stage 3 deep sleep; sleepwalking / night terrors arise here 9.9 Personality — theories & types Approach One thing to remember Big Five (OCEAN) Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism — the dominant trait model Eysenck Three dimensions: Extraversion, Neuroticism, Psychoticism (PEN); biologically based Cattell 16 PF ; source vs surface traits; factor analysis Allport Cardinal, central, secondary traits Freud (structural) Id (pleasure) – Ego (reality) – Superego (morality) Bandura Reciprocal determinism : person ↔ behaviour ↔ environment; self-efficacy Rogers Self-concept; congruence between real and ideal self; conditions of worth Locus of control (Rotter) Internal ("I control outcomes") vs external ("luck/fate does") 9.10 Intelligence — theories Theorist Model Spearman Two-factor: general g + specific s ; factor analysis Thurstone 7 primary mental abilities (no single g) Cattell-Horn Fluid (novel reasoning, declines with age) vs crystallised (knowledge, stable/rises) Gardner Multiple intelligences (linguistic, logical, musical, spatial, bodily, inter/intra-personal, naturalist) Sternberg Triarchic : analytical, creative, practical Goleman / Salovey-Mayer Emotional intelligence (perceive, use, understand, manage emotion) Cross-link: IQ scoring, deviation IQ, WAIS/WISC subtests live in §4 Assessment ; "scaled score 10 = 50th percentile" is your mock miss. 9.11 Freudian defense mechanisms Defense Quick example Repression Push a threatening thought out of awareness (the master defense) Denial Refuse to accept reality ("I'm not sick") Projection Attribute your own impulse to someone else ("you hate me") Displacement Redirect a feeling to a safer target (yell at the dog, not the boss) Sublimation Channel an impulse into a useful act (aggression → surgery/sport) — the "mature" one Reaction formation Act the opposite of the true feeling (hate disguised as overcare) Rationalisation Logical-sounding excuse for the real motive ("I didn't want it anyway") Regression Revert to an earlier developmental stage under stress Intellectualisation / Undoing Use abstract thinking to avoid the feeling / ritually cancel an act 9.12 Heuristics & cognitive biases Bias / heuristic What it is Availability heuristic Judge likelihood by how easily examples come to mind (plane crashes feel common) Representativeness Judge by resemblance to a prototype; ignores base rates Anchoring Over-rely on the first number/info given Confirmation bias Seek info that confirms what you already believe Framing effect Same info, different wording → different choice (90% survive vs 10% die) Hindsight bias "I knew it all along" after the outcome is known Functional fixedness / Mental set Can't see a novel use for an object / stuck on a strategy that worked before 9.13 Learning — fast contrasts Pair Difference Classical vs operant Pavlov: involuntary, stimulus pairing. Skinner: voluntary, consequences shape behaviour Positive vs negative Positive = add a stimulus; Negative = remove one. Reinforcement ↑ behaviour, punishment ↓ it Escape vs avoidance Escape ends an aversive stimulus already on; avoidance prevents its onset (your mock miss) Shaping / spontaneous recovery Reward successive approximations / an extinguished response briefly returns after a pause Conditioning detail (escape/avoidance, alliance, object relations) is in §5 ; emotion-theory and psychophysics rows are in 9.4 above. 9.14 Biostatistics rapid recall NIMHANS's biggest gap Cue Lock this Choosing the test — 2 groups, parametric independent t-test (paired data → paired t-test) 3+ groups, parametric ANOVA (one-way); repeated measures if same subjects 2 groups, non-parametric Mann-Whitney U (paired → Wilcoxon signed-rank) 3+ groups, non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis Two categorical variables Chi-square (Fisher's exact if cells small) Strength of a linear relationship Pearson r (parametric) / Spearman rho (ranks) Odds ratio / relative risk = 1 no association ; >1 = risk, <1 = protective (your mock miss) NNT = 1 / ARR ; ARR = control event rate − treatment event rate Type I error (alpha) false positive — reject a true null Type II error (beta) false negative — keep a false null; power = 1 − beta p-value P(data this extreme if null true). NOT the probability the null is true Sensitivity vs specificity Sensitivity = true-positive rate ( SnNout , rules out); specificity = true-negative rate ( SpPin , rules in) PPV / NPV depend on prevalence ; sensitivity/specificity do not Skew Positive (right) skew: mean > median > mode ; tail points to the higher numbers Parametric assumptions normal distribution, homogeneity of variance, interval/ratio data r and r² r ranges −1 to +1; r² = proportion of variance explained ; correlation ≠ causation TRAP: "Data is plural" (one datum, many data). And p < 0.05 only means statistically significant, not clinically important or "null is false." 9.15 Assessment — reliability, validity & score conversions Item Lock this Reliability types test-retest (stability), inter-rater (between scorers), internal consistency ( Cronbach's alpha / split-half), parallel forms Validity types content, criterion ( concurrent + predictive ), construct ( convergent + discriminant ), face Reliability vs validity Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity; a test can be reliable but not valid, never valid without being reliable z-score mean 0 , SD 1 T-score mean 50 , SD 10 Deviation IQ (Wechsler) mean 100 , SD 15 (Stanford-Binet old = 16) Wechsler scaled subtest score mean 10 , SD 3 — so scaled score 10 = 50th percentile (your mock miss) Sten / Stanine sten mean 5.5 (SD 2); stanine mean 5 (SD 2) Normal curve 68 / 95 / 99.7 within 1 / 2 / 3 SD; percentile = % scoring at or below you 9.16 Abnormal — disorder → hallmark & first-line Disorder Hallmark · first-line Major depression 2+ weeks low mood/anhedonia · SSRI (+ CBT) Bipolar I (mania) 1+ week elevated mood · lithium / valproate (mood stabiliser); antidepressant alone can trigger mania Schizophrenia positive + negative symptoms, 6 months · antipsychotic; clozapine for treatment-resistant OCD obsessions + compulsions · SSRI (high dose) + ERP (exposure & response prevention) Panic disorder recurrent unexpected attacks · SSRI + CBT Specific phobia marked fear of object/situation · exposure therapy (systematic desensitisation) PTSD symptoms >1 month after trauma · trauma-focused CBT / EMDR; SSRI GAD 6 months excessive worry · CBT; SSRI/SNRI (buspirone) Borderline PD instability of mood/relationships/self, fear of abandonment · DBT ADHD inattention/hyperactivity · stimulants (methylphenidate) Trigger: "compulsions/rituals" → OCD & ERP. "fear of abandonment + DBT" → BPD. "treatment-resistant schizophrenia" → clozapine. 9.17 Neuro one-glance — cranial nerves, localisation, aphasia Item Recall 12 cranial nerves (order) O lfactory, O ptic, O culomotor, T rochlear, T rigeminal, A bducens, F acial, V estibulocochlear, G lossopharyngeal, V agus, A ccessory, H ypoglossal Sensory / motor / both " Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter Most " (S/M/B per nerve) Broca's aphasia non-fluent, effortful, comprehension intact · frontal (Broca's area) Wernicke's aphasia fluent but meaningless, poor comprehension · temporal (Wernicke's area) Conduction aphasia can't repeat · arcuate fasciculus Frontal lobe executive function, planning, personality (Phineas Gage) Hippocampus forming new long-term memories (H.M. → anterograde amnesia) Amygdala fear, emotional salience Cerebellum balance, coordination, motor learning Hypothalamus homeostasis, 4 F's, drives the pituitary 9.17a Motor control — who does what classic NIMHANS swap-trap Structure Job Lock the trap Premotor cortex plans externally / sensory-cued movement (see it, reach for it); preps posture before M1 fires premotor = external / cue-driven SMA (supplementary motor area) plans internally generated, self-initiated movement; sequencing from memory + bimanual coordination SMA = internal / from within (premotor vs SMA = external vs internal) Basal ganglia initiate / select / gate movement; set vigour , scale force & amplitude "scales force / amplitude" → basal ganglia · resting tremor (Parkinson's) · chorea = Huntington's Cerebellum timing, coordination, balance, error correction; compares intended vs actual and smooths on the fly "timing / smoothing / coordination" → cerebellum · intention tremor, ataxia, dysmetria Two traps: resting tremor = basal ganglia, intention tremor = cerebellum. "Force/amplitude" = basal ganglia, "timing/smoothing" = cerebellum. Full version on the biopsych cheatsheet §8 . 9.18 The Acts, founders & "X is to Y" Pairing Lock this Mental Healthcare Act 2017 (India) — decriminalised suicide, right to treatment, advance directive RPwD Act (Rights of Persons with Disabilities) 2016 — 21 disabilities, replaced the 1995 Act RCI Act (Rehabilitation Council of India) 1992 — regulates training of psychologists/therapists POCSO 2012 — Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Wundt : ___ first psychology lab (1879) Binet : ___ first practical intelligence test (mental age) Aaron Beck : ___ cognitive therapy / cognitive triad Carl Rogers : ___ client-centred therapy Joseph Wolpe : ___ systematic desensitisation Beck vs Ellis cognitive triad / collaborative empiricism vs REBT / ABC, more confrontational 9.19 Language — grammar traps & one-word substitutions Trap The fix Subject-verb agreement "Each / every / neither / one of" takes a singular verb; "a number of" = plural, "the number of" = singular Either/neither ... or/nor verb agrees with the nearer subject Fewer vs less fewer = countable, less = uncountable Between vs among between = two, among = three or more Lie vs lay lie (recline, no object) vs lay (put down, takes an object) One-word: fear of enclosed spaces claustrophobia (open/public spaces = agoraphobia) One-word: study of populations demography One-word: one who knows many languages polyglot One-word: incapable of being corrected incorrigible One-word: bitter attack in speech/writing diatribe (vs panegyric/eulogy = praise) Highest fast-marks section — grammar and vocab are pure recall, no reasoning. Deeper drills in §7 . Exam-day rules Longest option is often correct on these papers, but only as a tiebreaker, never over knowledge. "NOT" / "EXCEPT" questions — circle the NOT, you're hunting the odd one out. This is where tired people lose marks. Negative marking −0.25: answer if you can eliminate 2 options; skip a pure blind guess. Don't change a first instinct unless you find a concrete reason to. That's the whole syllabus on one page. Read it through once tonight, then on a second pass just the tables and the red trap boxes. Everything you flagged in the mocks is inlined here. You already scored 91.25 — tonight is about locking what you know , not learning new things. Stop early, sleep, trust yourself tomorrow. Sihan MET 2026 + NIMHANS prep · /notes/textbook/ · the one self-contained source · built 2026-05-22

title: Mock Debriefs & Weak-Spot Fixes
text: Mock Debriefs & Weak-Spot Fixes Every concept you got wrong, guessed, or flagged across all the mocks (MET Mock 1, the NIMHANS PYQ-based mock, the diagnostic-baseline drills, and the MPhil/PEP sets) consolidated into one corrective read, organised by topic, not by which mock it came from. Where a miss recurred across mocks it is marked as a persistent weak spot. This is where you fix what tripped you. Nothing is cut: every corrected answer, distractor analysis, mnemonic, and exam trap from the originals lives here, merged so each concept appears once. In this book The recurring weak spots (read first) Exam-day execution rules Biopsychology & neuroanatomy Neurochemistry, endocrine & pharmacology Famous cases & amnesias Assessment, IQ history & tests Research methods & biostatistics Psychotherapy: who founded what Abnormal psychology & classification Social psychology & the self Developmental psychology Cognitive: memory, learning, psychophysics, creativity Language & verbal reasoning MPhil layer: ethics, law, culture, MSE The recurring weak spots (read first) Across every mock the same clusters bled marks. These are your real syllabus, ranked by how often and how badly they recurred. Each links to its full fix below. Weak spot Where it recurred The fix in one line Pituitary / hypothalamus / endocrine axis NIMHANS mock (3 of 6 biopsych wrongs), diagnostic baseline FLAT PiG anterior pituitary; melatonin is pineal; cortisol is adrenal cortex , not medulla; hypothalamus integrates endocrine + autonomic Neuroanatomy: tracts, lobes, basal ganglia MET Mock 1 (6 biopsych wrongs) Corticospinal crosses at medullary pyramids; right parietal → left neglect; red nucleus is NOT basal ganglia Therapy school attribution MET Mock 1 (4 wrongs), NIMHANS (3 wrongs) Match technique → school → founder by trigger word; empty chair = Perls, musterbation = Ellis, therapeutic community = Maxwell Jones Standard scores & WAIS structure Both mocks, diagnostic Subtest scaled M=10 SD=3; index M=100 SD=15; +1 SD = 84th pct; VCI + PRI = 3 core subtests each Reliability statistic ↔ concept NIMHANS, MET, diagnostic (Cohen's kappa missed twice) Kappa = inter-rater categorical; alpha/KR-20 = internal consistency; ICC = inter-rater continuous Sampling: stratified vs cluster vs non-probability MET Mock 1 + NIMHANS (quota/cluster swapped) Stratified = sample within strata; cluster = whole clusters; "can't compute sampling error" = non-probability (quota) ICD vs DSM durations NIMHANS (schizophrenia), MET (dysthymia, PTSD clusters) NIMHANS leans ICD: schizophrenia ≥1 month (ICD) vs ≥6 months (DSM); read which classification the stem names Named social-psych concepts NIMHANS (Genovese, Type D, anomie all wrong) Pure trivia: learn the named effect + its discoverer + its two-factor mechanism Sleep architecture (REM vs delta) Diagnostic (twice), MET Mock 1 (elimination) REM = atonia + wake-like EEG (paradoxical); delta/N3 = slow wave + normal tone; parasomnias (sleepwalking) are N3 "NOT / EXCEPT" negation-blindness Every mock — careless misses Underline the negation before reading options; this is your most expensive avoidable error High-yield Your self-notes are the syllabus. Every "wtf is X" / "never read this" / "don't know shit about this" you wrote on a question is a topic you had not opened. The same notes recurred across mocks, which means a gap left unfixed reappears. The NIMHANS mock sat at 71.25 vs an 80 cutoff (gap 8.75 = roughly 9 wrongs to convert); 6 of those wrongs were in biopsych alone, so fixing that one section clears the line. On MET Mock 1 your attempted-accuracy was 92% (49 right, 4 wrong) but you skipped 47 — there the gap was coverage, not accuracy. PYQ analysis of 300 NIMHANS questions (2023–25) shows Therapy + Abnormal + Biopsych together = ~49% of marks; that is where to spend time. Trap Your guessing is luck-loaded. On the NIMHANS mock you guessed ~17 times and got 14 right; that regresses toward ~50% on the real paper, so plan against a score nearer 68 than 71. A guess is only worth it on MET-style scoring (+4/−1) once you have eliminated 2+ options. Exam-day execution rules Underline NOT / EXCEPT / LEAST / ALL in the stem before reading options. Half your "knew it but got it wrong" misses are negation-blindness (the ACTH/melatonin pituitary question, the Bandura "not required" question). ~20% of NIMHANS PYQs are NOT-stems. On a NOT-question, pick the outlier , not the most familiar item. On antonym / odd-one-out items, find the outlier first. If 3 of 4 options agree in meaning, the 4th is almost always the answer (gregarious: 3 synonyms + reclusive). Read the relationship in the stem — synonym? antonym? part-whole? cause-effect? — before scanning options. Eliminate extreme-word options on RC main-idea questions: "every, always, never, all, none, only, must" are usually too strong. Pick the most general statement the passage actually supports. Hedging language ("can," "may," "in some cases," "a range of") → tone is "supportive but qualified," not absolute. If the stem names ICD, give ICD durations; if DSM, give DSM. If unspecified on NIMHANS, default to ICD (Indian exam). MET often leans DSM. Don't guess on biostats unless the RR/OR/HR/NNT table is firm. You were guessing 4–5 of 10 biostats questions — a coin flip on ~20% of NIMHANS marks. Pacing: 100 Qs / 90 min ≈ 54 sec/Q. Over 90 sec → mark and skip, return later. Don't change a first instinct unless you find a concrete reason. Last 5 minutes: never leave a blank where there is no negative marking; with −0.25, only answer if you eliminated 2 options. Length of options is not a reliable tell on the real paper — don't lean on it. NIMHANS uses heavy case-vignette stems; practise extracting the diagnostic core fast. Biopsychology & neuroanatomy This was the single biggest leak: 6 wrong on each of the two full mocks. You are not weak on biopsych in general — you are weak on where structures are , which side does what , and endocrine/neurology trivia . Lock
